scope: A 13-chapter systems course on Pipecat, the real-time voice-agent framework, built around TWO first-class learner goals plus a migration decision, and ordered so that no chapter argues from evidence a later chapter supplies. GOAL ONE — the composition theory, the 'lego block' spirit stated by name and anchored in code. The composition phase teaches Pipes-and-Filters (Garlan & Shaw 1993) and the hourglass narrow waist (Beck, CACM 2019) plus the Expression Problem (Wadler 1998) as the ideas that make 'I can add a process in the middle or remove it very easily' literally true in this repo: the uniform interface is one signature, `async def process_frame(self, frame: Frame, direction: FrameDirection)` at processors/frame_processor.py:820 plus `push_frame` at :1004; `def link()` at :671 has a three-statement body — two pointer assignments at :677-678 plus a `logger.debug` at :679 — and validates nothing; `Pipeline._link_processors` (pipeline.py:197-202) is a fold with `link` as the operator and validates nothing; and the algebra has real witnesses in the tree — `IdentityFilter` as the identity element, `NullFilter` as the (leaky) zero, `BasePipeline(FrameProcessor)` so pipelines nest, `ParallelPipeline` as the parallel combinator, `ServiceSwitcher(ParallelPipeline)` as a higher-order composition. The phase CLOSES on ch-03, which characterises the learner's own already-shipped realtime_voice as the concrete counter-design — a CLOSED union where Pipecat has an open sum type — so that every later comparison in the course draws on a baseline that has already been established rather than one that arrives at the end. GOAL TWO — how to design an agent on Pipecat, specifically how to carry boson-agent's layered rule system across. ch-10 reads `src/pipecat/flows/` as a state machine that deliberately lives OUTSIDE the pipeline (`FlowManager` at manager.py:80 is a plain class that drives the pipeline via `self._worker.queue_frames(...)`), and ch-12 — placed AFTER the latency budget in ch-11, because its decisive trade-off is denominated in milliseconds — gives the learner three constraints and makes him derive the rule-processor seam and the collapse-into-one-processor conclusion himself, with the verified finding that Flows does NOT require transitions to be LLM function calls (`await flow_manager.set_node_from_config(node_config)`, manager.py:588, is public and proven in-tree at examples/flows/warm_transfer.py:261 and multi_worker_handoff.py:352). THE MIGRATION PREMISE is a COMPARISON, not a port. The text-only gateway on branch lina-new-dental-dev has no server-side audio — barge-in reasons over text partial transcripts in gateway/interrupt/, its PartialDetector is dead code, and the real endpointer is a 2000 ms silence timer inside gateway/server/websocket.py. chapters.title: Pipes and Filters: The Uniform Interface That Makes Splicing Possible
chapters.summary: The 'lego block' feeling is not a metaphor and not Pipecat's invention — it is Garlan & Shaw's Pipes-and-Filters style, and the single property that produces it is the uniform interface. Their reuse claim is exact: any two filters can be hooked together provided they agree on the data transmitted between them. Pipecat makes that proviso trivially true by giving every processor the identical signature, `async def process_frame(self, frame: Frame, direction: FrameDirection)` (processors/frame_processor.py:820), paired with one write verb, `push_frame(frame, direction=FrameDirection.DOWNSTREAM)` (:1004), over a two-valued `FrameDirection` enum (`DOWNSTREAM = 1`, `UPSTREAM = 2`, :60-70). That is the entire contract, and 131 `process_frame` overrides across 117 files in `src/` all present the same shape. Splicing is therefore `list.insert(N, p)` on the argument to `Pipeline(...)`: `def link(self, processor)` is at :671 and its whole body is three statements — `self._next = processor` (:677), `processor._prev = self` (:678) and a `logger.debug` (:679) — that is, two pointer assignments plus a debug log, with no validation of any kind between them; and `Pipeline._link_processors` (pipeline/pipeline.py:197-202) is a five-line fold with `link` as the operator. There is no type check, no capability negotiation, and no ordering assertion anywhere in `src/pipecat/pipeline/`. THE ALGEBRA, with witnesses that actually ship: `IdentityFilter` (processors/filters/identity_filter.py:17) is the identity element — its whole body is `super().process_frame(...)` then `push_frame(frame, direction)`. `NullFilter` (filters/null_filter.py:18) is the zero, and instructively a *near*-zero: it must leak `SystemFrame` and `EndFrame` (:47-48) or the pipeline cannot start, interrupt, or shut down, which is exactly where the algebra meets reality. Associativity is a type fact — `class BasePipeline(FrameProcessor)` (base_pipeline.py:19) and `class Pipeline(BasePipeline)` (pipeline.py:91) — so a pipeline IS a processor and nests with no special case; Pipecat depends on that law in its own code, rebinding `pipeline = Pipeline([edge_source, pipeline, edge_sink])` at pipeline/worker.py:537. `ParallelPipeline` (parallel_pipeline.py:24) is the parallel combinator, `FunctionFilter` (filters/function_filter.py:21) the conditional, and `ServiceSwitcher(ParallelPipeline, Generic[StrategyType])` (pipeline/service_switcher.py:247) with `ServiceSwitcherStrategyManual`/`ServiceSwitcherStrategyFailover` is a higher-order composition — a pipeline parameterized by a strategy object. Substitutability is also why every processor is unit-testable: `pipecat/tests/utils.py:182` is a generic harness, `Pipeline([source, processor, sink])`, that works for any component precisely because position N has no type. THE PRICE, in two parts. (1) Every processor must tolerate every frame it does not care about, and Pipecat collects that tax in one mandatory line: `await super().process_frame(frame, direction)` first, unconditionally. The base implementation (`async def process_frame` at :820, last statement `await self.__resume(frame)` at :847) is not bookkeeping — it is the lifecycle: `StartFrame → __start()` (def at :1091), whose entire body is a call to `__create_process_task()` at :1097; `InterruptionFrame → _start_interruption()`; `CancelFrame → __cancel()`. Skip it and `StartFrame` never creates the process task, so the processor accepts frames forever and emits nothing: a silent black hole with no exception and no warning. This contract is unwritten — a grep of every `*.md` in the repo for `super().process_frame` returns zero hits; it is enforced by 107 call sites and by nothing else. (2) 'Any processor anywhere' is a type-level truth and a semantic lie: `Pipeline([transport.input(), tts, llm, transport.output()])` links, starts, runs, and is silently wrong, because `tts` receives no `TextFrame` from an LLM that sits downstream of it. Nothing raises; the bot is just silent. The chapter ends with the position-N checklist the type system will not run for you: lifecycle, transparency, base-class identity, upstream supply, downstream demand — and the discipline of telling 'this processor is broken' apart from 'this position is wrong'. CONTRASTED against boson-agent, which has no seam: a turn is one function, `run_agent_loop(runtime, user_input) -> AsyncIterator[StreamEvent]` (basement/loop/agent_loop.py:176), 561 lines around `while turn_count < runtime.config.max_turns:` (:207-209) ending at `break` (:363). Adding a step means editing that `while` body, and a function call is the opposite connector from a pipe — the caller names the callee and they share the `runtime` object outright, violating both Garlan-Shaw invariants. What boson buys for that is real and should be said: one totally-ordered greppable control flow, cancellation read at exactly two sites (:344, :513), and a stack trace instead of a frame vanishing at an unknown hop. That is the whole comparison this chapter makes; the second counter-design, the learner's own realtime_voice, is ch-03's subject and is deliberately not previewed here.

Three algebra panels with live proofs: insert `IdentityFilter` anywhere and diff the output frame stream against the un-spliced run (byte-identical, a provable no-op); insert `NullFilter` and watch data frames die while `SystemFrame` and `EndFrame` still leak through, with a 'make it a true zero' toggle that blocks `EndFrame` and hangs the shutdown; and a nesting view that wraps a sub-`Pipeline` as a single element, then re-wraps it the way `pipeline/worker.py:537` does, showing that grouping is free because `BasePipeline(FrameProcessor)`. Two failure presets are the payoff. 'Wrong order' builds `Pipeline([transport.input(), tts, llm, transport.output()])`, links and starts it cleanly, and produces silence with no error anywhere — the ordering constraint has no home in the type system. 'Forgot super()' removes the mandatory first line from one processor and animates `StartFrame` arriving at `__start` (:1091), the `__create_process_task()` call at :1097 never firing, and the queue filling forever. chapters.title: The Narrow Waist: Frame as a Sum Type and What It Costs
chapters.summary: Lego blocks are the symptom; the hourglass is the cause. Processors are interchangeable only because exactly one datatype crosses every boundary — `Frame`. Plurality lives above (62 service DIRECTORIES under `src/pipecat/services/`, plus 11 loose `.py` modules alongside them) and below (11 transport provider packages, and 7 concrete `FrameSerializer` implementations); the middle is singular. The literature is named and dated: the hourglass figure from CSTB/NRC, *Realizing the Information Future* (1994); Deering's 'Watching the Waist of the Protocol Hourglass' (ICNP '98) which made 'narrow waist' standard vocabulary; Beck's 'On the Hourglass Model' (CACM 62(7), 2019) with the Deployment Scalability Trade-off — generality at the waist is bought by *removing* capability, not adding it; Akhshabi & Dovrolis (SIGCOMM '11) showing the waist ossifies precisely so the layers above and below can innovate; and Wadler's 'The Expression Problem' (12 Nov 1998) for the bill. The waist is minimal exactly as Beck predicts: `Frame` (frames/frames.py:65) carries no payload at all — `id`, `name`, `pts`, `broadcast_sibling_id`, `metadata`, `transport_source`, `transport_destination`, every one `field(init=False)`. The three-way split under it is NOT a taxonomy of content but a scheduling contract, and the docstrings say so: `SystemFrame` (:105) 'takes higher priority ... not affected by user interruptions'; `DataFrame` (:116) 'processed in order ... cancelled by user interruptions'; `ControlFrame` (:128) same ordering, for settings and flush-then-end. Two honest findings the chapter states rather than smooths over: at runtime the split is really two-way — `isinstance(frame, DataFrame)` appears zero times in the whole `src/pipecat` tree — so Data-versus-Control is a documentation convention; and the taxonomy leaks, because `LLMContextFrame` (:551) subclasses `Frame` directly, in no branch, landing in the default-priority bucket by fallthrough. THE COST, measured at this commit by AST walk rather than grep: `frames.py` is 2,415 lines and holds 129 top-level `ClassDef`s, of which 122 transitively inherit `Frame`; subtracting the three branch classes themselves leaves 119 CONCRETE frame types. (Getting this right requires normalising subscripted bases before the fixed point — `class ServiceUpdateSettingsFrame(ControlFrame, UninterruptibleFrame, Generic[TSettings])` at frames.py:2251 is invisible to a walk that reads `ast.ClassDef.bases` literally, which silently drops its three subclasses out of the hierarchy.) The 7 top-level classes that are NOT `Frame` descendants are worth naming because they are the ones a reader miscounts: `Frame` itself, `UninterruptibleFrame` (a mixin), `AudioRawFrame`, `ImageRawFrame`, `DTMFFrame`, `FunctionCallResultProperties` and `FunctionCallFromLLM`. The branch split is 46 `SystemFrame` descendants, 33 `DataFrame`, 40 `ControlFrame` (46+33+40 = 119, since `LLMContextFrame` sits in no branch and `InputTextRawFrame` sits in two). Repo-wide the concrete frame count is 150 = those 119 plus 31 defined outside `frames.py` — counting top-level classes only; `frames.py` also nests 4 more inside functions (`EndTaskFrame`, `StopTaskFrame`, `CancelTaskFrame`, `InterruptionTaskFrame`), which would make it 154 — whose three largest homes are `processors/frameworks/rtvi/frames.py` (9), `transports/daily/transport.py` (8) and `services/openclaw/frames.py` (6). The dispatch tax is 577 `isinstance(frame, ...)` sites across 136 files. That is Wadler's table with the rows exploding. Adding a COLUMN — a processor — is nearly free and composes with everything. Adding a ROW — a frame — is free for the pipeline and a liability for every processor, because `FrameProcessor.process_frame` (:820-847) handles only `StartFrame`, `InterruptionFrame`, `CancelFrame` and the pause/resume pair: THERE IS NO AUTOMATIC PASS-THROUGH, so an unknown frame is silently dropped by any processor whose author did not anticipate it. Pipecat chose columns and that is right: a streaming framework's growth vector is new vendors, weekly, while the media vocabulary (audio/text/image/context) is stable. Beck's ossification warning is the flip side — `Frame`'s field set is now effectively unchangeable, which is why the escape hatch is the untyped `metadata: dict` and not a new base field, and why the in-flight 1.8.0 deprecations are actively *stripping* configuration off `StartFrame` into `FrameProcessorSetup` so frames carry only data. THE LOAD-BEARING PRECEDENT, stated in one sentence and then cashed as a rule rather than explored: `src/pipecat/flows/` is exactly boson's case — a conversation state machine with nodes, transitions and actions — and it added EXACTLY TWO frames, both `ControlFrame` subclasses and neither in `frames.py`: `FunctionActionFrame(ControlFrame)` (flows/actions.py:50) and `ActionFinishedFrame(ControlFrame)` (:63). (How that package actually works is ch-10's subject, not this chapter's.) So the rule for every boson concept is: subclass `ControlFrame`, do not touch `DataFrame`. And the rule generalises into a three-way test applied before any boson concept enters the pipeline: state (current stage, rule results, script cursor) is NOT a frame — it lives in a plain manager object; effects ARE existing frames (stage prompt → `LLMUpdateSettingsFrame`, tool swap → `LLMSetToolsFrame`, scripted utterance → `TTSSpeakFrame`, rule verdict → `LLMMessagesAppendFrame`); and only a genuinely new in-band signal that must be ordered against speech, by a processor that is not the stage manager, earns a class in `boson/frames.py`. Budget two to four total, matching flows' two and openclaw's six; use `frame.metadata` for correlation IDs and stage tags. A tenth new frame means you re-implemented boson's internal protocol inside Pipecat's waist and lost the interchangeability you came for.

chapters.title: What You Already Built: realtime_voice as the Baseline
chapters.summary: MECHANISM AND EVIDENCE ONLY. This chapter characterises the learner's own shipped system so that every later comparison in the course has an established baseline to draw on; it casts NO keep/replace/hybrid votes, states no preference and reaches no verdict. All of that is ch-13's job, and deferring it is deliberate. `packages/realtime_voice/` on branch voice-chat-dev is 3,886 lines of source plus 1,504 lines of tests and 60 test functions, against Pipecat's 168,847 lines of source and 92,538 lines of tests with 4,236 `def test_` matches. THE FRAMING QUESTION, and the reason this chapter closes the composition phase: ch-02 taught an OPEN sum type — anyone can add a `Frame` subclass, at a dispatch cost paid across 577 `isinstance` sites. realtime_voice made the opposite bet. Its unit of data is a CLOSED union, `VoiceRuntimeEvent = VADEvent | ASREvent | AgentTextDelta | VoiceEvent` (types.py:201), so adding an event type means editing that one line plus every `isinstance` chain that consumes it, including `transport/webrtc/transport.py:_control_event`, which raises `TypeError` on anything outside the union. Ask the learner which bet each design made and what each one buys: the open sum type buys third-party extension without touching the core and pays with silent drops; the closed union buys exhaustiveness — a type checker can prove every case is handled and an unknown event is a loud `TypeError` rather than a frame vanishing at an unknown hop — and pays by making the core the only place extension can happen. Both are defensible; they are optimising for different populations of author. THE REST OF THE MECHANISM, feature by feature, in both directions. Processor abstraction: realtime_voice has none — one `VoiceSession` (561 L) whose `_supervise()` opens a single `asyncio.TaskGroup` with exactly two long-lived tasks for the WHOLE session (Pipecat's per-processor runtime is ch-04's subject); there is no `link()`, no `FrameDirection`, no upstream push, and shutdown is 24 hand-sequenced lines instead of an `EndFrame` propagating, with `_STOP = object()` sentinels standing in for the frame Pipecat already has. Five swappable `Protocol` slots exist, but the VAD→ASR→agent→TTS order is hardcoded: slots are replaceable, the topology is not — which is precisely the property ch-01 said Pipes-and-Filters buys and this design forgoes. VAD: `SileroVADConfig(threshold=0.5)` with a two-state `self._speaking` bool, no volume AND-gate, no idle-mic timeout, and `ValueError('SileroVAD requires 16 kHz mono PCM')` so there is NO 8 kHz telephony path; a two-frame blip becomes a real `SPEECH_STARTED` that immediately advances the generation and cancels the assistant. Streaming STT: absent entirely — `OpenAICompatibleUnaryASR` buffers the whole utterance into a WAV and makes one `audio.transcriptions.create` call at `finalize()`, and `ASREventKind.INTERIM`/`END_OF_TURN` are declared but emitted only by a test fake. Breadth: 2 providers against 62 service directories, 1 transport against 11 provider packages, 0 telephony serializers against 6, no renegotiation or ICE restart, and essentially no observability — `provider_latency_ms` and `endpoint_latency_ms` fields plus a `discarded_frames` counter that nothing reads. WHAT PIPECAT SHIPS NO EQUIVALENT OF, stated with the same neutrality. `KoreanPhraseChunker` (283 L): a 1→2→bounded-tail adaptive batching schedule (`_batch_phase` 0/1/2), `_is_safe_period` refusing to split `1.5`, `...`, `gpt-4.1` and hostnames, `_is_numeric_separator` protecting `1,000`, and `_INTERNAL_TAG` stripping gateway control tags from spoken text while preserving source character spans. `AudioTextPlayoutLedger`: `audible_text()` reconstructs the heard character prefix by sample ratio and therefore works with a TTS that emits no timestamps at all, at the cost of being a linear char-per-sample approximation mid-word; `playout_complete()` is what distinguishes 'the customer interrupted me' from 'I finished and they replied' via the `semantic_interrupt` flag. `WebRTCSessionManager`: `secrets.token_urlsafe(32)`, SHA-256 digest with `hmac.compare_digest`, a 15-minute TTL, and one-live-peer enforcement raising `SessionConflictError` unless `reconnect=True` — explicit reconnect, no silent takeover. `ControlEvent` v1: dotted-type validation, strict in-order `sequence` checking that raises on a gap, a 64 KiB cap, and a recursive `_reject_audio_payload` that bans audio from the control channel on principle. `GenerationAudioQueue.discard_generation()`: a hand-rolled `deque` plus `asyncio.Condition` written for the one thing `asyncio.Queue` cannot do — atomic filtered rebuild under the lock. And `StreamingConversationAgent`, which yields only `AgentTextDelta` so stages, rules and tools stay text-native in basement and gateway — the slot that ch-09 will show has no Pipecat analogue. PARITY, named as parity: barge-in and cancellation reach the same guarantee by different mechanisms — generation-ID equality checked at six sites plus `BoundedAudioOutput.activate_generation()`, against one interruption signal cascading through N processors that each cancel their own task. TEST NAMES AS EVIDENCE, because maturity is an input the course will need later: 6 files, 1,504 lines, 60 test functions at a 0.39 test:src ratio (Pipecat's is 0.55), and the names are the tell — `test_confirmed_barge_in_purges_server_audio_and_cancels_old_work`, `test_barge_in_event_precedes_slow_provider_cancellation`, `test_playout_acknowledgement_returns_only_heard_prefix`, `test_late_playout_ack_cannot_extend_interrupted_audible_prefix`, `test_next_turn_after_completed_playout_is_not_an_interruption`, `test_each_generation_has_exactly_one_terminal_event`, `test_ingress_overflow_rejects_frame_instead_of_growing_latency`, `test_dots_inside_ascii_identifier_are_not_sentence_boundaries` — plus a real aiortc loopback test and a pinned regression for the PyAV uninitialized-memory bug that made 'silence' come out as full-scale random PCM. `realtime_voice/testing/fakes.py` ships six deterministic doubles as PUBLIC API: determinism was designed in, not retrofitted. The chapter ends by handing forward a fact sheet, not a recommendation.

chapters.title: What Runs When You Call worker.run(): Queues, Tasks, and Out-of-Band Priority
chapters.summary: ONE LINA SALES CALL is the running example, and every constant in this chapter answers a question that call raises. A Korean customer connects to a FastAPI host over a websocket; the host creates a `PipelineWorker` per session and hands it to a long-lived `WorkerRunner`. The customer hangs up mid-sentence. The bot finishes its closing line. The customer goes silent for four minutes. Each of those is a different shutdown or timeout path with a different constant, and by the end of the chapter the learner owns the process/session/worker topology for the Lina host — which is a DELIVERABLE later chapters consume rather than re-invent. THE VOCABULARY, corrected first. `PipelineWorker(BaseWorker)` (pipeline/worker.py:198) and `WorkerRunner(BaseObject, BusSubscriber)` (workers/runner.py:83) are the real runnable units; `PipelineTask(PipelineWorker)` (worker.py:1482) and `PipelineTaskParams(WorkerParams)` (:1498) are `@deprecated` 1.3.0 aliases scheduled for removal in 2.0.0, so any tutorial written against `PipelineTask` is stale. The rename has a stated reason (AGENTS.md:82): 'a worker is a runnable unit, task now refers only to asyncio tasks, and cross-worker RPC uses jobs and job groups.' The worker owns lifecycle; the runner owns process concerns — signals, the bus, and ending when every worker is done. FOR THE LINA HOST SPECIFICALLY, `auto_end=False` is mandatory and the source says why in as many words: the `auto_end` contract is documented at runner.py:263-266 ('When `True` (the default), the runner ends once every root worker has finished. When `False`, the runner blocks until `end` or `cancel` is called'), and the rationale at :250-253 — 'For long-lived hosts that add and remove workers over many sessions (e.g. a FastAPI server), pass `auto_end=False`' — is exactly the Lina topology, because the process outlives any one call. `WorkerRunner` adds `add_workers(*workers)` (:199-235), `run(worker=None, *, auto_end=True)` (:237-319), idempotent `end`/`cancel` (:332-366), and SIGINT/SIGTERM routing to `_sig_cancel` (:529-537). WHAT ACTUALLY RUNS INSIDE ONE PROCESSOR — the mechanics that make the rest of the course legible. Each `FrameProcessor` owns TWO QUEUES and TWO TASKS, not one. `FrameProcessorQueue(asyncio.PriorityQueue)` (frame_processor.py:132) declares `START_PRIORITY = 1`, `SYSTEM_PRIORITY = 10`, `DEFAULT_PRIORITY = 20`, and `put()` (:152-171) assigns them by `isinstance` plus a monotonic `__counter` that preserves arrival order within a tier and stops the queue from ever comparing unorderable dataclass frames. Then `__input_frame_task_handler` (:1287-1313) is the whole trick: `if isinstance(frame, SystemFrame): await self.__process_frame(...)` INLINE, else relay into `__process_queue`, drained by a separate and CANCELLABLE `__process_frame_task_handler` (:1315-1333). A system frame overtakes in-flight data twice — by priority on the way in, and by never entering the slow queue at all. `_enable_direct_mode` (:717-719) is a third path that skips both, and `__create_process_task` (:1222) returns immediately when it is set. `FrameQueue.reset()` (utils/frame_queue.py:84-95) drains every non-`UninterruptibleFrame` item and re-enqueues the uninterruptible ones with `_uninterruptible_count` kept O(1). THE TWO THEORY PARAGRAPHS THIS CHAPTER OWNS. First: control latency in a pipeline is QUEUE DEPTH divided by drain rate, not code speed. A strictly ordered pipe has one channel, so a stop message enqueued at time t is delivered only after everything ahead of it drains; with N items and a sink draining at realtime rate r, control latency is N/r no matter how fast your handler runs. That single sentence is why a priority tier exists at all, and it is the arithmetic ch-08 will spend. Second: BACK-PRESSURE IS PHYSICALLY IMPOSSIBLE against a live microphone. Reactive Streams defines back-pressure as the mechanism that lets mediating queues be bounded; Pipecat's queues are unbounded, and the evidence is a grep — `grep -n maxsize` over `frame_processor.py`, `frame_queue.py`, `base_input.py`, `base_output.py` returns ZERO hits, with `base_input.py:265` a bare `asyncio.Queue()`. Blocking the producer does not pause the speaker; it relocates the buffer and grows latency monotonically. A realtime media pipeline's only two options are DROP or FLUSH, and Pipecat chooses selective flush triggered by an out-of-band signal. (What that flush cascade actually does to TTS, the audio clock and the carrier's playout buffer is ch-08's subject, taught once, there, where the learner already owns the output queue.) THE FOUR PATHS OFF ONE LINA CALL. (a) Setup and start: `run(params)` (:748-791) does `_setup_within_timeout` (:1104-1121; on timeout it fires `on_setup_timeout` and cleans up without ever pushing a frame, bounded by `SETUP_TIMEOUT_SECS = 20.0`) → `_create_tasks()` → `_wait_for_pipeline_finished()`, and the engine is `_process_push_queue` (:1205-1246), which constructs the `StartFrame`, queues it, blocks on `_pipeline_start_event` under `START_TIMEOUT_SECS = 20.0`, and on timeout logs 'being blocked somewhere?' and refuses to run. Your pipeline is re-wrapped on the way in: `self._pipeline = Pipeline(processors, source=source, sink=self._sink)` (:549) where `processors` is `[self._rtvi, pipeline]` when RTVI was auto-created (:548), plus a further `Pipeline([edge_source, pipeline, edge_sink])` when `bridged` is set (:522-537) — the ch-01 associativity law being cashed by the framework itself. (b) The customer hangs up mid-sentence: `cancel(*, reason=None)` (:739-746, where `reason` is KEYWORD-ONLY — `async def cancel(self, *, reason: str | None = None)` — so `cancel("hangup")` is a `TypeError`) → `_cancel` (:973-984) queues a `CancelFrame`, and `_wait_for_pipeline_end` (:1063-1091) BOUNDS that wait by `cancel_timeout_secs`, `CANCEL_TIMEOUT_SECS = 20.0`. (c) The bot finishes its closing line: `stop_when_done()` (:730-737) queues an `EndFrame` and the same function leaves that wait UNBOUNDED by design — 'Ending flushes what is queued, so cutting the wait short would drop the audio the EndFrame exists to play out.' Memorize the asymmetry: violent path bounded, graceful path unbounded. (d) The customer goes silent: `IDLE_TIMEOUT_SECS = 300` with `cancel_on_idle_timeout=True` and `idle_timeout_frames=(BotSpeakingFrame, UserSpeakingFrame)` — five minutes of dead air before the worker is cancelled, which is ABSURD for a sales call where thirty seconds is already a lost customer, and the retune is a constructor kwarg, not a patch: pass your own `idle_timeout_secs` and a narrower `idle_timeout_frames` tuple. The plumbing is `IdleFrameObserver` (:106-140) setting an event on `StartFrame` or any `idle_timeout_frames`, `_idle_monitor_handler` (:1401-1415) waiting on it, and `_idle_timeout_detected` (:1417-1441) cancelling the worker and optionally the whole runner via a `BusCancelMessage`. One more mechanism the later chapters actually spend: `queue_frame` (:793-808) is direction-split, so a DOWNSTREAM frame enters at the HEAD via `_push_queue` while anything else enters at the tail via `self._sink` — which is the fact that makes ch-10's `FlowManager` injection and ch-12's transition race legible. `ParallelPipeline` exists and this course does not use it. The chapter closes on the canonical voice pipeline — `transport.input(), stt, user_aggregator, llm, tts, transport.output(), assistant_aggregator` (examples/getting-started/06-voice-agent.py:81-91) — read as a data-dependency chain, with the observation that nothing runs at all until `worker.queue_frames([LLMRunFrame()])` fires from `on_client_connected` (:107-114) — and then states the Lina topology as a deliverable: one FastAPI process, `WorkerRunner(auto_end=False)` created once at startup, one `PipelineWorker` per call added via `add_workers` and removed on disconnect, every session an `asyncio.Task` on the same loop.

MIDDLE PANEL opens ONE processor and renders its two queues and two tasks separately: `__input_queue` as a priority queue with the 1/10/20 tiers visible and a monotonic counter column proving intra-tier FIFO, `SystemFrame`s executed INLINE on the input task, everything else relayed into the cancellable `__process_queue`. Inject a `SystemFrame` mid-stream and watch it overtake twice — by priority on the way in, and by never entering the slow queue at all — with a `_enable_direct_mode` switch that bypasses both and a `FrameQueue.reset()` button that drains everything except the `UninterruptibleFrame`s. chapters.title: Transports: WebRTC, WebSocket, and Telephony-as-a-Serializer
chapters.summary: The layer that would replace gateway/server/ (1,404 lines: websocket.py, protocol.py, access.py, history.py, interruption.py). Nothing here needs `PipelineWorker`: a transport is a pair of processors, so the real prerequisites are the uniform interface and the frame taxonomy, not the runtime. `class BaseTransport(BaseObject)` starts at transports/base_transport.py:96 and the file ends at :137, so it is a 42-line class in a 137-line file, and it declares exactly two abstract methods — `def input()` at :122 and `def output()` at :131, each returning a `FrameProcessor` — so swapping Daily for SmallWebRTC changes the connection object and the params class, not the pipeline. There are 11 provider PACKAGES under `src/pipecat/transports/` and 13 `BaseTransport` subclasses repo-wide, since some packages ship more than one. THE CENTRAL CORRECTION: THERE IS NO TELEPHONY TRANSPORT. `ls src/pipecat/transports/` at this commit returns `base_input.py`, `base_output.py`, `base_transport.py`, `daily/`, `heygen/`, `lemonslice/`, `livekit/`, `local/`, `moq/`, `smallwebrtc/`, `tavus/`, `vonage/`, `websocket/`, `whatsapp/` — no twilio, telnyx, plivo, exotel or sip directory. A phone call is `FastAPIWebsocketTransport` plus a provider-specific `FrameSerializer` under `src/pipecat/serializers/`, of which there are exactly 7 concrete implementations — 6 telephony (twilio.py 314 L, telnyx.py 292 L, plivo.py 256 L, exotel.py 171 L, genesys.py 964 L, vonage.py 188 L) plus protobuf.py; `base_serializer.py` is the ABC and does not count. The framework's own runner proves the architecture: `_create_telephony_transport` (runner/utils.py:486) sets `params.serializer = TwilioFrameSerializer(...)` and returns `FastAPIWebsocketTransport(websocket=websocket, params=params)` at :554. That serializer is simultaneously the codec boundary, the resample point, the call-control client and the DTMF decoder — five of six telephony providers default to 8 kHz (`twilio_sample_rate: int = 8000`, telnyx/plivo/exotel/genesys the same; only Vonage is 16 kHz), and μ-law is 8-bit companded, so the Nyquist ceiling on the wire is 4 kHz and upsampling to 16 kHz restores sample count, not bandwidth. For Lina TMR that is the governing constraint on Korean STT accuracy, since the fricative/sibilant band and much of the 받침 discrimination cue sit at or above 4 kHz and are simply not present in the signal. Also corrected: `TransportParams` no longer has a `vad_analyzer` field at all — the CHANGELOG removed it from `TransportParams` and every transport input class, and the live mount points are `LLMUserAggregatorParams.vad_analyzer` and the standalone `VADProcessor`. Call lifecycle detail worth carrying: two different IDs per provider (`stream_sid` echoed on every outbound media and clear message vs `call_sid` only for REST call control), `auto_hang_up: bool = True` on Twilio/Telnyx/Plivo firing on `EndFrame`/`CancelFrame`, barge-in flushing the carrier buffer with `{"event": "clear"}`, and asymmetric DTMF — inbound works everywhere via `InputDTMFFrame(KeypadEntry(digit))`, outbound has no serializer support at all and falls back to `_write_dtmf_audio()` pushing synthesized tone WAVs as ordinary audio. On the WebSocket side, `FastAPIWebsocketTransport` (websocket/fastapi.py:611) receives an already-accepted socket, so you own the route, handshake and auth; `FastAPIWebsocketParams` adds exactly six fields including `serializer` and `ws_close_timeout: float = 0.5`; and with no serializer set, every inbound message is silently dropped. The non-obvious part is that a WebSocket has no playback clock, so the transport fabricates one — `self._send_interval = (self.audio_chunk_size / self.sample_rate) / 2` (:456) and a `_write_audio_sleep()` whose comment says it exists 'to emulate an audio device.' Then the honest accounting against the learner's TWO existing implementations: the text-only gateway/server/, of which roughly 700 lines (access.py's 374 L of bearer/subprotocol auth and principal-to-session binding, history.py's debug projection, the generation-based dispatch protocol) have no Pipecat counterpart; and realtime_voice/transport/webrtc/, ~960 lines already landing where `SmallWebRTCTransport` lands, on the same aiortc, with the two things ch-03 named that Pipecat ships neither of — `WebRTCSessionManager` HMAC session authorization with a 15-minute TTL and one-live-peer enforcement, and a versioned, sequence-checked, audio-forbidden `ControlEvent` schema. Adopting Pipecat's transport buys telephony and ten other provider packages plus renegotiation and ICE restart; it costs re-implementing both of those as application code.
chapters.figure_spec: The same bot behind four stacks side by side: Daily/SmallWebRTC, raw WebSocket, WebSocket-plus-Twilio-serializer, and the learner's own realtime_voice aiortc transport. Show the packet path, where the jitter buffer and codec sit, and added latency per hop. The decisive panel is the telephony one: expand the serializer as its own box and animate one frame crossing it — 8 kHz μ-law in, resample to 16 kHz, an interruption signal out as a provider clear event — with a Nyquist band chart marking the 4 kHz ceiling against the Korean fricative and 받침 cue bands. A counting strip states the inventory precisely: 11 transport provider packages, 13 `BaseTransport` subclasses repo-wide, 7 concrete `FrameSerializer` implementations (6 telephony + protobuf, with `base_serializer.py` greyed out as the ABC). A capability matrix underneath marks, per stack, what boson's gateway/server/ and realtime_voice each already provide and what has no equivalent on the other side.

chapters.title: When Does the User's Turn End? VAD, Streaming STT, and the Turn-Strategy Chain
chapters.summary: ONE QUESTION ORGANISES THIS ENTIRE CHAPTER: when is the user's turn over? Everything here is an answer to it at a different layer, and the layers are taught in dependency order — the audio-level answer first, the transcript-level answer second, and the strategy chain that arbitrates between them third. Nothing later in the course may be denominated in a VAD quantity that has not been taught by the end of this chapter. PART ONE — THE AUDIO-LEVEL ANSWER: VAD. Voice activity detection is split three ways — a model (`SileroOnnxModel`, silero.py:34, per-chunk confidence), a four-state hysteresis machine (`VADAnalyzer`, vad_analyzer.py:63, `VADState.QUIET/STARTING/SPEAKING/STOPPING`), and an edge-triggered event emitter (`VADController`, vad_controller.py:31, which fires only on transitions into terminal states so `STARTING`/`STOPPING` are never observable outside the analyzer). `VADParams` has exactly four fields — `confidence = 0.7`, `start_secs = 0.2`, `stop_secs = 0.2`, `min_volume = 0.6` — and the gate is an AND (`speaking = confidence >= params.confidence and volume >= params.min_volume`), which is why you tune barge-in with the timing params and not the threshold. Seconds become frame counts in `VADAnalyzer.set_params`, whose `def` is at vad_analyzer.py:151, and the arithmetic is worth doing by hand because it is easy to get wrong: `vad_frames_per_sec = self._vad_frames / self.sample_rate` at :162, so at 16 kHz with 512-sample chunks that is 512/16000 = 0.032 s per chunk; then `self._vad_start_frames = round(self._params.start_secs / vad_frames_per_sec)` at :164 gives `round(0.2 / 0.032)` = `round(6.25)` = **6** consecutive chunks, not 7, and `self._vad_stop_frames = round(self._params.stop_secs / vad_frames_per_sec)` at :165 computes the stop side identically. Silero supports 8 kHz natively (`num_frames_required()` returns 256), and 256/8000 is also 0.032 s, so the counts come out IDENTICAL at both rates — Lina TMR's telephony audio, which ch-05 established is 8 kHz μ-law on five of six carriers, needs no VAD retuning. Crucially, Silero decides 'there is voice' and a STRATEGY decides 'this is a turn': the controller broadcasts `VADUserStartedSpeakingFrame`, and `VADUserTurnStartStrategy` converts it into a real turn start — which is part three. A MECHANISM DIFFERENTIAL against ch-03's realtime_voice, written as a differential and deliberately with no comparative adjective and no recommendation, because ch-13 is the only place either design is scored: Pipecat runs four states with a `min_volume` AND-gate, a `STARTING → QUIET` path that returns to quiet without ever emitting a start, native 8 kHz support, and an `audio_idle_timeout`; realtime_voice runs a two-state `self._speaking` bool at `threshold=0.5`, with no volume gate, no idle-mic timeout, and a hard `ValueError('SileroVAD requires 16 kHz mono PCM')` so there is no 8 kHz path at all. Fed the same two-frame blip, the first returns to `QUIET` and emits nothing; the second emits `SPEECH_STARTED`, which advances the generation and cancels the assistant. State both behaviours, state which product situations each behaviour is a liability in, and stop there. PART TWO — THE TRANSCRIPT-LEVEL ANSWER: STREAMING STT. Server-side speech recognition as a frame source. Three base classes in `stt_service.py` (1,040 L): `STTService(AIService)` (:51), `SegmentedSTTService(STTService)` (:797), `WebsocketSTTService(STTService, WebsocketService)` (:929), with one abstract method whose `def` is at :335 — `async def run_stt(self, audio: bytes) -> AsyncGenerator[Frame | None, None]` (:334 is the `@abstractmethod` decorator, not the signature). Streaming sends every ~20 ms chunk straight to the socket; segmented accumulates into `_audio_buffer`, trims to a 1-second pre-roll covering the detection lag part one just quantified as six chunks, and on `VADUserStoppedSpeakingFrame` wraps the buffer with `pcm_to_wav` and calls `run_stt` once. `STTService` itself never emits an `InterimTranscriptionFrame` — the file contains zero references to it and 25 provider modules construct it directly; the base class only intercepts `TranscriptionFrame` in `push_frame` (:519) to stamp `finalized` and close the TTFB window. Pipecat also redefines TTFB as speech-end to final transcript (`_handle_vad_user_stopped_speaking`, :627, computing `speech_end_time = frame.timestamp - frame.stop_secs` — a subtraction that only means anything now that `stop_secs` has been taught) and broadcasts each service's measured P99 in an `STTMetadataFrame` so downstream timers can size themselves. PROVIDER SELECTION HAPPENS HERE AND NOWHERE ELSE IN THE COURSE, so the benchmark table is built once, in this chapter, and every later chapter that needs a number references it rather than re-rendering it. `stt_latency.py` (68 L) is the repo's only hard benchmark table and it holds 23 provider constants, not the dozen usually quoted — so quote the whole table or stop calling a subset exhaustive. In full: `DEEPGRAM 0.35`, `DEEPGRAM_SAGEMAKER 0.35`, `SONIOX 0.35`, `ELEVENLABS_REALTIME 0.41`, `ASSEMBLYAI 0.42`, `GRADIUM 0.62`, `SPEECHMATICS 0.74`, `CARTESIA 0.81`, `SARVAM_REALTIME 1.00`, `TOGETHER 1.00`, `SARVAM 1.17`, `GLADIA 1.49`, `GROQ 1.54`, `GOOGLE 1.57`, `SMALLEST 1.59`, `OPENAI_REALTIME 1.66`, `AZURE 1.80`, `MISTRAL 1.89`, `AWS_TRANSCRIBE 1.90`, `ELEVENLABS 2.01`, `OPENAI 2.01`, `FAL 2.07`, `XAI 2.14` — with `DEFAULT_TTFS_P99 = 1.0` for local models (`NVIDIA` and `WHISPER` are aliases of it), a real spread of 0.35 s to 2.14 s, and every constant measured at `VADParams.stop_secs=0.2`, the value part one derived six chunks from. Korean-specific provider choice, with the open unknown STATED rather than guessed: 12 services carry a verified `Language.KO` mapping — Soniox, Speechmatics, Gladia, Google, Azure (azure/common.py:200), AWS Transcribe, Nvidia Riva, ElevenLabs (sending the three-letter `"kor"`), xAI, Fal, and the local Whisper and Moonshine — plus FunASR, which is a thirteenth Korean-capable service by a DIFFERENT mechanism and must be described that way: it has no `Language.KO` mapping at all, only a plain string set, `_FUNASR_LANGUAGES = {"zh", "en", "ja", "ko", "yue", "nospeech"}` (funasr/stt.py:42), with anything outside it coerced to `"auto"`. Deepgram is a PASSTHROUGH with no `LANGUAGE_MAP` at all so the repo takes no position on it despite its joint-best 0.35 s latency, AssemblyAI's map has no Korean entry, `CartesiaTurnsSTTService` is English-only at launch, and `SarvamSTTService`'s only `KO*` key is `Language.KOK_IN` — Konkani, an easy misread. No accuracy number and no 8 kHz telephony number exists anywhere in the tree for any service or language. PART THREE — THE ARBITER: THE TURN-STRATEGY CHAIN, which consumes both of the previous parts. THE STRUCTURAL CORRECTION: there is no endpointing.py, no EndpointingConfig, and no single turn-detector class. The real subsystem is `src/pipecat/turns/` — 4,429 lines across start strategies, stop strategies, a `UserTurnController` that can veto, and mute strategies — wired not on the transport and not on the VAD but on `LLMUserAggregatorParams` (llm_response_universal.py:120), which exposes `user_turn_strategies`, `user_mute_strategies`, `user_turn_stop_timeout: float = 5.0`, `user_idle_timeout`, `vad_analyzer` and `audio_idle_timeout: float = 1.0`. That the `vad_analyzer` mount point is a field on the AGGREGATOR params rather than on the transport is the single most surprising wiring fact in the voice-I/O phase, and it is the direct consequence of the CHANGELOG removal ch-05 already recorded. The defaults are `start = [VADUserTurnStartStrategy(), TranscriptionUserTurnStartStrategy()]` — one strategy per part of this chapter, audio and transcript — and `stop = [TurnAnalyzerUserTurnStopStrategy(turn_analyzer=LocalSmartTurnAnalyzerV3())]`, so THE DEFAULT STOP STRATEGY IS THE ML SMART-TURN ANALYZER, an audio-only ONNX classifier (`smart-turn-v3.2-cpu.onnx`) over Whisper log-mel features that never reads transcript text; VAD-only (`SpeechTimeoutUserTurnStopStrategy`, `user_speech_timeout: float = 0.6`) is the downgrade you must explicitly select. Note the asymmetry: `SmartTurnParams.stop_secs = 3` is the analyzer's own silence fallback, but the model is consulted at every VAD stop — which part one established is 0.2 s and six chunks — so the ML verdict is the normal path, not the exception. Both timing strategies compute an STT safety net as `effective_stt_wait = max(0.0, self._stt_timeout - self._stop_secs)` from the `STTMetadataFrame.ttfs_p99_latency` part two introduced, short-circuited by `TranscriptionFrame.finalized`, and both warn if `stop_secs != 0.2` because every constant in the 23-entry table was measured at that value. SOME PROVIDERS TAKE THE TURN DECISION AWAY FROM THE CHAIN ENTIRELY, and the count and the classification both matter. There are NINE assignment sites of `frame.user_turn_strategies = ExternalUserTurnStrategies(...)` inside `service_metadata_frame()` across EIGHT service files — `sarvam/stt.py` has two, one per service class — and only TWO of the nine are unconditional. UNCONDITIONAL (external endpointing is the default): `CartesiaTurnsSTTService` (cartesia/turns/stt.py:198) and Deepgram Flux (deepgram/flux/stt_base.py:250). PROVIDER-FLAG-GATED, all seven of them, with the exact guard: Speechmatics (speechmatics/stt.py:561, under `if is_given(mode) and mode != TurnDetectionMode.EXTERNAL` on `self._settings.turn_detection_mode`); Gladia (gladia/stt.py:370, `if self._settings.enable_vad`); Soniox (soniox/stt.py:422, `if not self._vad_force_turn_endpoint`); AssemblyAI (assemblyai/stt.py:669, `if not self._vad_force_turn_endpoint` — the SAME flag as Soniox, and both docstrings say so in the same words: 'In the default Pipecat mode (`vad_force_turn_endpoint=True`) the STT proposes no turns'); `SarvamSTTService` (sarvam/stt.py:395, `if self._settings.vad_signals`); `SarvamRealtimeSTTService` (sarvam/stt.py:1034, `if self._endpointing == "vad"`, which is default-on and therefore the one flag-gated site that behaves unconditionally out of the box); and OpenAI (openai/stt.py:414, `if self._server_vad_enabled`, which is off by default because `turn_detection=False`). So: 9 sites, 8 services, 2 unconditional, 7 provider-flag-gated — and DO NOT put Soniox and AssemblyAI in different groups, since they are gated on the identical `vad_force_turn_endpoint` flag with identical default behaviour. (A separate and different mechanism exists on three realtime LLM services — inworld, xai and openai realtime pass `user_turn_strategies=ExternalUserTurnStrategies()` as a CONSTRUCTOR kwarg rather than assigning it on a metadata frame; they are not STT services and are not part of this count.) That is the mechanism that would let boson's `PartialDetector` be deleted outright rather than merely replaced. This re-founds boson's text-partial assumption on real audio — 2000 ms of text silence becomes 0.6 s plus smart-turn — and it re-founds ch-03's baseline too: realtime_voice has NO streaming STT, only `OpenAICompatibleUnaryASR` buffering the whole utterance to WAV for one blocking call at `finalize()`, with `ASREventKind.INTERIM` emitted only by a test fake. That blocking call sits on the critical path whether or not Pipecat is adopted; ch-13 is the only place it is scored.
chapters.figure_spec: THREE STACKED PANELS IN THE CHAPTER'S OWN ORDER, all driven by one Korean utterance on one shared time axis, so the reader sees the same turn decided three times at three layers. PANEL ONE — VAD. Run the audio through the four-state machine with `VADState.QUIET/STARTING/SPEAKING/STOPPING` lit as it transitions, sliders for all four `VADParams` fields, and the AND-gate drawn as two meters (confidence and volume) that must BOTH clear before `speaking` is true. The frame-count arithmetic is shown live as a worked calculation rather than an answer — `def set_params` at :151, `vad_frames_per_sec = 512/16000 = 0.032` at :162, `round(0.2/0.032) = round(6.25) = 6` at :164, and the stop side computed the same way at :165 — with a sample-rate switch to 8 kHz / 256 samples that recomputes to the SAME 6, proving Lina's telephony audio needs no retuning. A two-frame false-start blip injector runs the same input through Pipecat's machine and through realtime_voice's two-state `self._speaking` bool at `threshold=0.5`: the first returns `STARTING → QUIET` and emits nothing, the second emits `SPEECH_STARTED` and cancels the assistant. Both outcomes are reported as BEHAVIOUR with no scoring, no badge, no winner — the panel has no comparative label anywhere in it. PANEL TWO — STREAMING STT. Audio streams in while interim transcripts appear, get revised, and finalize, with timestamps, against a segmented service that emits nothing until `VADUserStoppedSpeakingFrame` and then makes one blocking call. The provider selector is the COMPLETE 23-constant `stt_latency.py` table rendered as a sorted bar chart from `DEEPGRAM 0.35` to `XAI 2.14`, with `DEFAULT_TTFS_P99 = 1.0` marked as the local-model fallback and `NVIDIA`/`WHISPER` drawn as aliases of it, so no subset is implied to be exhaustive. THIS IS THE ONLY PLACE IN THE COURSE THAT TABLE IS BUILT AS AN INTERACTIVE CONTROL; ch-11's waterfall consumes the selected value and must not re-render the table. chapters.title: Streaming TTS: First Audible Sample, Word Timestamps, and Korean
chapters.summary: Speech synthesis as a frame sink, and why the whole design optimises one number. `TTSService(AIService)` (tts_service.py:109, 2,136 L) is not text-in-audio-out — it is a reordering buffer that owns sentence aggregation, a per-turn audio-context FIFO driven by a single `_serialization_queue: FrameQueue` (:405), and word-timestamp bookkeeping. STATE THE REAL LADDER, because the usual shorthand does not cover the tree. `tts_service.py` defines EIGHT service classes: `TTSService` (:109), `WordTTSService` (:1882), `WebsocketTTSService` (:1899), `InterruptibleTTSService` (:1969), `WebsocketWordTTSService` (:2040), `InterruptibleWordTTSService` (:2062), `AudioContextTTSService` (:2083) and `AudioContextWordTTSService` (:2121). The inheritance is a two-branch tree, not a single chain: `WordTTSService(TTSService)` and `WebsocketTTSService(TTSService, WebsocketService)` both hang off the root; `InterruptibleTTSService(WebsocketTTSService)`; `WebsocketWordTTSService(WebsocketTTSService)`; `InterruptibleWordTTSService(InterruptibleTTSService)`; `AudioContextTTSService(WebsocketTTSService)`; `AudioContextWordTTSService(AudioContextTTSService)`. The four `Word` classes are deprecated since 0.0.105 because word-timestamp functionality is now always active — but note that the 'everything with Word in the name is deprecated' escape clause does NOT collapse the tree, because `AudioContextTTSService(WebsocketTTSService)` at :2083 has no 'Word' in its name, is not deprecated, and is a fourth live class alongside `TTSService`, `WebsocketTTSService` and `InterruptibleTTSService`. So the live ladder a subclass author actually chooses from is those four, and the axes are two — websocket transport, and per-turn audio contexts — not one. The metric that matters is not TTFB but TTFA — time to first AUDIBLE sample, where `TTFAMetricsData` reports `ttfa`, `ttfb` and `leading_silence` with `ttfa = ttfb + leading_silence` — because a provider that pads 150 ms of silence looks perfect on byte-level monitoring and sounds slow. Total synthesis throughput is nearly irrelevant: audio plays at 1x wall clock, so everything after the first chunk is produced underneath playback and costs the listener nothing. Only the gap from 'LLM decided' to 'first audible sample' is exposed, and it is the sum of three things this layer controls — aggregation delay, provider TTFB, and leading silence. Sentence aggregation is a named, separately-measured budget line (`TextAggregationMetricsData`), and `TextAggregationMode.SENTENCE` (the default) will not call `run_tts` until a boundary is confirmed AND a non-whitespace lookahead character has arrived, to tell `"$29."` from `"$29. Next"` — one extra token of latency per sentence, by design, with its own docstring budgeting 200-300 ms. Korean matters here twice: `UNAMBIGUOUS_SENTENCE_ENDING_PUNCTUATION` (utils/string.py:125) is the fallback used specifically because NLTK does not support Korean; and `processors/aggregators/sentence.py`'s standalone `SentenceAggregator` is a DECOY — it is a separate `FrameProcessor` that `TTSService` never touches. Word and sentence boundaries: there is no `WordBoundaryFrame` and no `TTSWordFrame`; word-level information rides on `TTSTextFrame.pts` in nanoseconds (frames.py:417), one frame per word token emitted as the word is spoken, alongside `AggregatedTextProgressFrame` for highlighting. That matters downstream, because word timestamps are what let a barge-in truncate the assistant context at the last SPOKEN word rather than the last generated token — the mechanism ch-08 spends. Korean narrows the field hard: twelve TTS services map `Language.KO`, but `resolve_language` FAILS SILENTLY — it falls back to the base code with a warning — so a Korean bot pointed at Rime (word-timestamp capable, five languages, no Korean) configures fine and produces garbage, with the only downstream catch being `max_consecutive_zero_audio_contexts: int = 3`. Intersecting Korean support with word timestamps leaves exactly six services: Azure, Cartesia, ElevenLabs, Inworld, Soniox, xAI. STATE THE PROVENANCE OF THAT NUMBER HONESTLY: it is the intersection of two greps over this tree — services whose language map contains `Language.KO`, and services that emit word-timestamped `TTSTextFrame`s — and it is a claim about what the CODE declares, NOT a claim verified by listening to output or by any behavioural test. A service could declare Korean and synthesise it badly, or emit timestamps that drift; nothing in the repo would catch either. There is no maintained self-hosted Korean TTS — the only local service with a Korean map is `XTTSService`, deprecated since 1.7.0 with 'No replacement', and neither Kokoro nor Piper maps Korean — so on-prem Korean TTS is a gap, not a choice, and no Korean-native provider (Typecast, Supertone, Naver Clova) is integrated. One subtle finding: Korean is deliberately excluded from the CJK word-grouping paths (both Cartesia and ElevenLabs test `base_lang in {"zh", "ja"}`), so it falls through to the space-separated branch and gets per-token frames — which matches 어절 spacing but is an untested assumption in this code. Compared against realtime_voice's `KoreanPhraseChunker` (283 L) from ch-03, which has no Pipecat equivalent: the 1-then-2-then-bounded-tail adaptive batching schedule, `_is_safe_period` guards against splitting `1.5`, `gpt-4.1` and hostnames, `_is_numeric_separator` for `1,000`, and internal-tag stripping that preserves source character spans. Also maps boson's interrupt/fillers.py, which despite the name is user-side filler SUPPRESSION over `(text, agent_status)` and survives untouched.

chapters.title: Barge-In and the Interruption Cascade
chapters.summary: ONE IDEA, TAUGHT ONCE: what happens between the moment the framework decides the user has interrupted and the moment the last already-spoken byte stops coming out of the customer's phone. The DECISION that an interruption has occurred is not this chapter's subject — ch-06 taught that, at all three of its layers — and neither is provider selection. This chapter starts one instant later, from a turn-start signal that already exists, and it is placed here rather than earlier because the cascade is unteachable until the reader owns the TTS output queue and its clock task (ch-07) and the per-processor two-queue runtime (ch-04). THE CASCADE, with two corrections. First: `StartInterruptionFrame` and `StopInterruptionFrame` DO NOT EXIST — a grep returns zero hits. There is a single field-less `InterruptionFrame` (frames.py:1142), a `SystemFrame` with no fields, broadcast in BOTH directions by `broadcast_interruption()` (frame_processor.py:1017-1022) → `broadcast_frame(InterruptionFrame)` (:1038-1054), which constructs TWO instances, cross-links them via `broadcast_sibling_id`, and pushes one each way. And `EndFrame` is NOT a `SystemFrame` — `class EndFrame(ControlFrame, UninterruptibleFrame)` (frames.py:1899) — so graceful end is deliberately in-band and only the violent `CancelFrame` (:999) rides the priority channel, which is the cleanest evidence that ch-04's data/signal split is design and not convenience. There is no central coordinator: the cascade is EMERGENT, with every processor independently running `_start_interruption()` (:1130-1150) from the base `process_frame` and cancelling its own task via `__cancel_process_task()` (:1149) — while that task is INSIDE your `process_frame()`, at an arbitrary `await`. That is the price ch-04 warned about, cashed: adjacency is a lie, and a processor that appends on frame A and flushes on frame B can be killed between them, leaving a half-full accumulator that emits last turn's fragment on the next turn. Pipecat hits this in its own code and pays for it explicitly at services/tts_service.py:1041, `self._aggregated_frame_sequencer.clear()  # discard all pending slots on interruption`. There is no LLM abort API either: `LLMService._handle_interruptions` (llm_service.py:758-761) only cancels tool calls marked `cancel_on_interruption`; the generation dies because cancelling the process task raises `CancelledError` inside the provider's streaming `async for`, which is why the `finally` block's `LLMFullResponseEndFrame` is NEVER pushed for an interrupted turn. TTS stops in two layers — the service clears every accumulator and resets the serialization queue (tts_service.py:1030-1066), and websocket subclasses bounce the socket entirely because a half-spoken server-side context cannot be rewound. Then the output transport cancels the clock and video tasks (`MediaSender.handle_interruptions`, base_output.py:566-593) and allocates a brand-new `asyncio.PriorityQueue` (base_output.py:1067-1071), discarding every queued not-yet-due timed frame. Flushing your own queue is NOT sufficient: `serializers/twilio.py:187` emits `{"event": "clear", "streamSid": ...}` because bytes already on the wire live in Twilio's playout buffer, beyond your reach. The chunking constants explain the granularity: `audio_out_10ms_chunks: int = 4` (transports/base_transport.py:72) and `audio_bytes_10ms = int(self._sample_rate / 100) * channels * 2` (base_output.py:135-136) make 40 ms of PCM per written chunk, and the source comment says the quiet part out loud — 'If we receive long audio frames we will chunk them. This will help with interruption handling.' Chunk size IS an interrupt-granularity decision, and with the `_audio_queue` (base_output.py:690) filled by a TTS vendor at burst rate but drained by `_clock_task_handler` (:1079) at realtime, a 3-second Korean sentence arriving in ~400 ms leaves ~75 chunks resident — which is ch-04's N/r arithmetic producing a ~3 s in-band stop delay, and the reason the signal must be out-of-band. GStreamer got here first and Pipecat vendors it (`processors/gstreamer/pipeline_source.py:39`): its docs draw exactly this line between events serialized with the buffer flow and out-of-band events 'skipping ahead of buffers being processed or queued in the pipeline', with `FLUSH_START` out-of-band and `EOS` serialized — buffers:events :: DataFrame:SystemFrame, EOS-is-serialized :: EndFrame-is-a-ControlFrame. SECOND AND LARGER CORRECTION: there is no truncation routine. Pipecat never had the untruncated text in the context, because the assistant aggregator sits AFTER `transport.output()` and is fed by audio-paced word-timestamped frames — `TTSTextFrame.pts` puts each word in `_clock_queue`, and `_clock_task_handler` sleeps until presentation time before pushing it — so the aggregator only ever saw text that was actually audible. Truncation is a property of pipeline POSITION, and `LLMContext` is interruption-unaware by design (grep for 'interrupt' in llm_context.py returns nothing). And what replaces the interrupted turn is nothing: `push_aggregation` writes an ordinary `{"role": "assistant", "content": <spoken-so-far>}` with no tag, no ellipsis and no `interrupted` field — `interrupted=True` lives only on the transient `AssistantTurnStoppedMessage` event payload, which is for transcript observers, not for the LLM. If zero text was aggregated the turn vanishes from history entirely. That is a real behavioural gap, since a bare partial reads to the model as a complete short reply, and it is confirmed by `tests/test_context_aggregators_universal.py::test_interruption`. THE AUTHOR'S OBLIGATIONS follow directly: reset every accumulator you own on `InterruptionFrame`, keep `SystemFrame` handling fast because it runs on the input task, always call `super().process_frame`, mark must-not-drop frames with the `UninterruptibleFrame` mixin (frames.py:147), use `has_queued_frame(frame_type)` (:1244), and remember `_cancelling` (:253) makes `queue_frame` return early (:714-715) so your frames vanish after a `CancelFrame`. Compared against boson's 581-line text-based interrupt subsystem, where every decision point takes `text: str`, `PartialDetector` is constructed once and its field never read anywhere (dead code), the real gate is a 2000 ms silence timer plus `InterruptionGate.allows`, `WordFilterPolicy(max_chars=3)` silently ignores '네' and '아니요' by CHARACTER count, and `cancel_during_streaming(partial_text)` writes `f"{partial_text}[interrupted-by-user]"` while `handle_barge_in` synthesizes a `ToolResultBlock` for every unanswered `tool_use` to keep strict role alternation. boson's barge-in is in-band BY CONSTRUCTION — the interrupt cannot even be CREATED until an STT partial exists, which is signal-origination latency sitting upstream of everything Pipecat optimizes, so moving the signal onto the priority channel without first moving its origination onto VAD buys nothing. And against ch-03's realtime_voice, which reaches PARITY by a different mechanism — generation-ID equality at six sites plus `AudioTextPlayoutLedger.audible_text()` reconstructing the heard character prefix by sample ratio, giving explicit truncation that works even with a timestamp-less TTS, at the cost of being a linear char-per-sample approximation mid-word. THE CLOSING SECTION IS A MECHANISM DIFFERENTIAL AND CONTAINS NO COMPARATIVE ADJECTIVE, no 'better', no 'wins', no 'should': on truncation accounting, Pipecat derives the spoken prefix from pipeline POSITION plus word-timestamped `TTSTextFrame.pts` released by the output clock, and records it as an untagged ordinary assistant message (or nothing at all, if no word played); realtime_voice derives it from a sample-ratio reconstruction in `AudioTextPlayoutLedger.audible_text()` that needs no timestamps from the TTS but approximates linearly mid-word, and records it explicitly with a `semantic_interrupt` flag; boson appends the literal marker `[interrupted-by-user]` to a partial that only exists once an STT partial has arrived. Three mechanisms, three different failure modes, three different dependencies on the TTS provider — write all three down, note which observation would distinguish them on real Korean traffic, and cast nothing. ch-13 is the only place any of them is scored.

The timeline BEGINS at an interruption signal that already exists — there is no VAD control anywhere in this figure, because the detection layer was built and made interactive in ch-06's `turn-boundary.html`, and a small caption points there rather than re-rendering it. chapters.title: Two Agent Loops: Who Owns the Context, the Tools, and the End of a Turn
chapters.summary: The hardest decision in the course, and ONE coherent idea: loop ownership. (Context compaction is a different subsystem with different failure modes and is deliberately not here — `LLMContextSummarizer` versus boson's `gateway/compact/` is on ch-13's give-back list.) Pipecat's message list is owned by one plain `LLMContext` (llm_context.py:83) that application code constructs and holds — three fields, `_messages`, `_tools`, `_tool_choice` — and the LLM service is entirely stateless with respect to history, reading whatever arrives on an `LLMContextFrame`. Two aggregators straddling the LLM mutate that one shared object in place, built over the same context by `LLMContextAggregatorPair` (llm_response_universal.py:2251). And `get_messages()` deliberately returns the LIVE list, not a copy (only `truncate_large_values=True` deep-copies), BECAUSE the assistant aggregator rewrites tool-result placeholders in place: `_handle_function_call_in_progress` appends a `{"role": "tool", "content": "IN_PROGRESS", "tool_call_id": ...}` placeholder and `_update_function_call_result` (:2157) later walks the live dicts and assigns `message["content"] = result` on the matching id. That inverts the usual defensive-copy instinct and is the single sharpest incompatibility with boson's `ContextManager`, whose `get_messages()` returns `deepcopy(self._messages)` specifically to prevent external mutation — a naive port silently breaks the tool-result path. There is no multi-turn tool loop inside the service and no turn cap anywhere: a service performs exactly one inference per `LLMContextFrame` — the entry point is `src/pipecat/services/openai/base_llm.py`, where `:599` is the mandatory `await super().process_frame(frame, direction)`, `:601` is `if isinstance(frame, LLMContextFrame):`, `:603` pushes `LLMFullResponseStartFrame()`, `:604` calls `start_processing_metrics()`, and the completion actually starts at `await self._process_context(frame.context)` on `:605` — fires any tool calls, and returns; the loop is closed by the PIPELINE, with the assistant aggregator pushing `LLMContextFrame` UPSTREAM (:1889) after results settle. Think-act-observe is a topology, not a `while` block, and `grep -rn "max_turns\|max_iterations\|max_tool_calls" src/pipecat/` returns zero hits — the only bounds are per-call `function_call_timeout_secs` or a per-tool `timeout_secs`. So boson's `max_turns=50` guard and its `while/else` exhaustion path have no counterpart and must be rebuilt as a counting `FrameProcessor` over `FunctionCallsStartedFrame` or consciously dropped. Also stale in the original plan: `create_context_aggregator()` DOES NOT EXIST at this commit (zero hits in `src/` and `examples/`; the CHANGELOG documents its removal alongside `OpenAILLMContext`), and `register_direct_function` is `@deprecated` since 1.4.0 in favour of `LLMContext(tools=[...])`. Registration has three routes that all land in `self._functions`: a direct function whose docstring supplies the schema via `DirectFunctionWrapper`, a `FunctionSchema(..., handler=...)`, or explicit `register_function(name, handler, ...)` with `function_name=None` installing a catch-all; and `_sync_registered_tool_handlers(frame.context.tools)` re-registers advertised handlers on EVERY context frame, marking them `auto_registered` so they can be pruned. Handlers never return a value — they `await params.result_callback(result)` — and both `FunctionCallInProgressFrame` and `FunctionCallResultFrame` are `UninterruptibleFrame` by design, because 'once a result is generated we always want to update the context.' Per-provider differences live behind `BaseLLMAdapter.to_provider_tools_format` in `src/pipecat/adapters/services/`, which is 3,647 L across 12 provider adapter modules; the whole of `src/pipecat/adapters/` is larger — 4,549 L across 19 files — so attach the number to the right path. Against this sits boson's `agent_loop.py` (561 L) with its `ToolRouter` and meta-tool dispatch (`use_tool`, `use_skill`), where three gates are deliberately kept separate — exposure (what the model sees, pinned to two entries under `maximize_caching` because the prompt-cache prefix is ordered tools → system → messages), availability (the `_allowed_tools_var` ContextVar per-stage allowlist checked inside `dispatch`), and permission (`PermissionChecker.check_tool`) — none of which Pipecat's registry has. And boson's `Message.role` is `Literal["user", "assistant"]` only: there is NO tool role, tool results ride as `ToolResultBlock` inside a user message, so porting to OpenAI-shaped `{"role": "tool", "tool_call_id": ...}` dicts is a schema rewrite, not a rename. Three resolutions are developed and costed: adopt Pipecat's loop and port tools to `FunctionCallParams` plus the `result_callback` contract (22 tool signatures change, sequential execution must be re-asserted because Pipecat defaults `run_in_parallel=True`); wrap boson's loop inside a single custom `FrameProcessor`; or bypass Pipecat's LLM service entirely and use it only for voice I/O. Ch-03 already showed the learner has ALREADY CHOSEN THE THIRD — `StreamingConversationAgent` yields only `AgentTextDelta` and tools stay text-native in basement and gateway via `GatewayConversationAgent` — which makes this the deepest architectural collision in the course, not a hypothetical. The chapter costs all three and hands the choice, unresolved, to ch-13.

Then toggle adopt / wrap / bypass and show concretely what breaks under each: the missing turn ceiling, the tool-role schema rewrite, the three separate boson gates (exposure, allowlist, permission) that Pipecat's registry has no slot for, and — under bypass — exactly which Pipecat processors remain in the pipeline. No option is marked recommended; the three costs are laid out for ch-13 to price.

chapters.title: Pipecat Flows: A State Machine That Lives OUTSIDE the Pipeline
chapters.summary: Pipecat ships a conversation state machine, and the single most important fact about it is architectural: `FlowManager` (flows/manager.py:80) is a PLAIN CLASS, not a `FrameProcessor`. It is not in the `Pipeline` list — in `examples/flows/hello_world.py:135-167` the list contains transport / stt / aggregators / llm / tts and no flow object; the `PipelineWorker` is built, `runner.add_workers(worker)` runs, and only then is `FlowManager(worker=worker, llm=llm, context_aggregator=context_aggregator, transport=transport)` constructed and kicked off from a transport event handler. It drives the pipeline FROM OUTSIDE via `await self._worker.queue_frames([...])` (manager.py:709 for `LLMRunFrame`, :841 for the settings batch), and reads back through exactly one channel — `ActionManager.__init__` calls `worker.set_reached_downstream_filter((ActionFinishedFrame, FunctionActionFrame, BotStoppedSpeakingFrame))` and registers an `on_frame_reached_downstream` handler. Teach why that inversion matters: it is the ch-02 rule applied at scale (state lives in a plain manager object, effects ride existing frames), and it means the flow's frames enter at the HEAD of the pipeline and must traverse every upstream processor before reaching the LLM — which becomes the ordering hazard of ch-12. NEXT CORRECTION: `FlowConfig` does not exist at this commit. `grep -rn "FlowConfig"` returns zero hits, as do `static flow` and `dynamic flow` — there is no declarative flow document, no JSON edge table, no `initial_node` key. The package docstring states the design plainly: 'Pipecat Flows determines conversation structure at runtime.' Nodes are Python functions returning `NodeConfig`, and an EDGE IS NOTHING BUT the second element of the tuple a handler returns: `ConsolidatedFunctionResult = tuple[Any, NodeConfig | None | _NoResponse]` (types.py:266), where element 1 being a `NodeConfig` transitions, `None` stays and responds, and `NO_RESPONSE` (types.py:247, a module-level singleton compared BY IDENTITY, `next_node is NO_RESPONSE`) stays and stays silent. `_set_node(node_id, node_config)` (manager.py:602-723) is the whole machine, and its frame batch is the thing to memorize: `LLMUpdateSettingsFrame(delta=LLMSettings(system_instruction=role_message))` only if `role_message` is set (and it PERSISTS across nodes until another node sets one); then `LLMMessagesAppendFrame` versus `LLMMessagesUpdateFrame`, and THAT CHOICE IS THE ContextStrategy (`frame_type = LLMMessagesUpdateFrame if strategy in [RESET, RESET_WITH_SUMMARY] else LLMMessagesAppendFrame`, :831-836); then `LLMSetToolsFrame(tools=functions)` UNCONDITIONALLY at :839, so a node that declares no functions passes `NOT_GIVEN` and CLEARS the tool set; then `LLMRunFrame()` queued separately at :709, only if `respond_immediately` (default `True`). NODE STATE IS A STRING, NOT A STRUCT — get this right because ch-02 deliberately did not claim otherwise: `self._current_node: str | None = None` (manager.py:149) holds a node ID string and is assigned at :703 (`self._current_node = node_id`); it NEVER holds a `NodeConfig`. And of the two `flows/types.py` shapes, only `NodeConfig` is a `TypedDict` — `ContextStrategyConfig` (types.py:155-156) is a plain `@dataclass`. `NodeConfig` (types.py:182-237) is a `TypedDict(total=False)` whose keys are `task_messages` (the ONLY required one), `name`, `role_message`, `role_messages` (deprecated 1.5.0), `functions`, `pre_actions`, `post_actions`, `context_strategy` and `respond_immediately` — and a misspelled key such as `respond_immediatly` is silently ignored. `ContextStrategy` (types.py:134) is `APPEND` / `RESET` / `RESET_WITH_SUMMARY`, the third deprecated since 1.5.0 with a hard 5.0-second `asyncio.wait_for` around summary generation that SILENTLY falls back to `APPEND` on failure or timeout (manager.py:799-822) — use a pre-action pushing `LLMSummarizeContextFrame` instead. Actions are exactly THREE built-ins, registered in `ActionManager.__init__` at actions.py:104-106: `tts_say`, `end_conversation`, `function` — and the maintainers explicitly de-emphasize custom actions ('we're de-emphasizing custom actions in favor of `function` actions, which should meet most needs', actions.py:293-294), with a hard-coded wait table where `function` always blocks and custom types never do. Actions cannot choose the next node, cannot veto a transition and cannot return a value; a raising PRE-action does abort the node, because pre-actions run before `_update_llm_context`, but post-action failures cannot un-set it. WHAT FLOWS DOES NOT GIVE YOU: no transition-legality validation and no node registry. `_validate_node_config` (manager.py:867-898) checks exactly two things — `task_messages` present, and each `functions` entry callable or a `FlowsFunctionSchema`. There is NO from→to check anywhere; node identity is `node_config.get("name", str(uuid.uuid4()))`, so an unnamed node gets a throwaway UUID and `flow_manager.current_node` guards stop working; and `self._current_functions: set[str]` (:148) is assigned at :704 and NEVER READ IN `src/` — state the scope of that claim precisely, because it IS read at six sites in `tests/test_flows_manager.py` (lines 191, 319, 758, 759, 1174, 1203). So it is dead as a runtime gate but live as a test assertion surface, which is a weaker and more accurate statement than 'never read anywhere in the codebase'. Handler dispatch is by ARITY INTROSPECTION rather than typing: `_call_handler` (:394-441) reads `len(inspect.signature(handler).parameters)` and branches 0/1/else, warning once per process on the deprecated arities, and `flows/actions.py` does the same for action handlers — which is why Pipecat's own bound-method built-ins take the legacy branch and trip their own deprecation warning. `FlowResult` is DEPRECATED since 1.5.0 with 'No replacement.'; the upstream contract is plain `Any`. Six exported names are already scheduled for removal in 2.0.0, so anything built here should target only `NodeConfig` with a string `role_message`, `FlowsDirectFunction` or `FlowsFunctionSchema`, two-arg handlers, `flows_tool_options`, and `ContextStrategy.{APPEND, RESET}`. The chapter is taught through `examples/flows/insurance_quote.py` (380 L), because the learner sells insurance by phone: five node FACTORY FUNCTIONS, four tool edges plus one self-loop, with collected data baked into the next node's prompt by f-string at transition time (`create_quote_results_node(quote)` interpolating a pre-formatted premium so the model never says 'one hundred fifty point zero'), and three distinct channels carrying data forward — the function's return value visible to the LLM, `flow_manager.state` (a bare `dict[str, Any]`, invisible to the model, surviving context resets), and the f-string in `task_messages` which is the only channel that reliably steers the next utterance. The round trip is worth naming honestly: `state["age"] → next node's prompt → the model → back as an LLM-supplied function argument`, which works but is a real trip through the model, so anything the model must not paraphrase (a 주민등록번호, a policy code) should be read from `state` inside the handler rather than declared as a parameter. `patient_intake.py` shows the list-of-dict capture pattern where the LLM gets an acknowledgement and the app gets the payload; `restaurant_reservation.py` shows outcome branching and `respond_immediately=not wait_for_user` as the one-flag switch between outbound and inbound calls; `warm_transfer.py` supplies the escalation recipe. Mapped onto boson: `agents/test-lina-gateway/stage_config.py` already IS this graph — `stages[X]["tools"] → NodeConfig["functions"]` is direct, `_GLOBAL_TOOLS → FlowManager(global_functions=[...])` mixed in at every node, but `stages[X]["transitions"]` STOPS BEING DATA and `stages[X]["skills"]` has no Flows concept at all. And `ContextStrategy.RESET` is per-transition context truncation boson does not have today, since `_inject_stage` only ever appends, so a long intake conversation drags every prior stage's prompt through every later inference.
