chapters.title: The Latency Budget and the Observer Plane
chapters.summary: Voice-to-voice latency as an accounting problem, in the same spirit as the training-memory ledger — and the instrument that measures it, because the budget and the observer plane are one subject: an unmeasured budget is a guess. This chapter deliberately precedes the rule-layer design in ch-12, since ch-12's decisive trade-off is denominated in milliseconds and cannot be argued before the denominator exists. THE BUDGET. Every millisecond from user speech offset to first audible agent audio: the endpointing wait (`VADParams.stop_secs` plus the STT's measured P99 time-to-final-segment), STT finalization, rule-layer evaluation, LLM time-to-first-token, sentence aggregation as its own named budget line, TTS time-to-first-AUDIBLE-sample, network and jitter. The formula stated plainly: `stop_secs + max(0, TTFS_p99 - stop_secs) + LLM TTFB (+ thinking) + text-aggregation + TTS TTFA + transport`. The two biggest terms are not the LLM. Pipecat encodes the first as the 23 per-provider constants in `stt_latency.py` (68 L), the repo's only hard benchmark table — BUILT ONCE IN CH-06, where provider selection actually happens, and consumed here as a single term rather than re-enumerated: it spans 0.35 s (`DEEPGRAM`, `DEEPGRAM_SAGEMAKER`, `SONIOX`) to 2.14 s (`XAI`), with `DEFAULT_TTFS_P99 = 1.0` for local models, all measured at the `VADParams.stop_secs=0.2` ch-06 derived six chunks from — and the second as `TTFA = TTFB + leading_silence`, computed by buffering PCM and calling `detect_speech_onset`, capped at `_TTFA_MAX_BUFFER_SECONDS = 3.0`. TTFB alone is misleading and the source says so: `stop_ttfb_metrics` ends at the first output of any kind including reasoning tokens, which is why `TTFATMetricsData(ttfat, ttfb, thinking_time)` exists and why a turn that answers from a tool result reports twice. Teach which stages are serial and which overlap, and why the LLM is the term everyone optimises and rarely the term that dominates. THE OBSERVER PLANE is a second READ-ONLY plane over the frame graph rather than a logging convention, and it is the reason the budget is knowable at all: `BaseObserver` (observers/base_observer.py:90) has four hooks — `on_process_frame(FrameProcessed)`, `on_push_frame(FramePushed)`, `on_processor_setup(ProcessorSetUp)`, `on_pipeline_started()` — and sees every frame transfer WITHOUT being spliced into the pipe, which is exactly the non-adjacency property boson's `SignalQueue` needs and which ch-12 will reach for. Services emit typed `MetricsData` as `MetricsFrame`s and the same stream feeds console logs, OpenTelemetry spans, Sentry transactions and the RTVI wire protocol, so you instrument by subscribing, not by editing processors — and `can_generate_metrics()` returns `False` on the base class, so only services that opt in report. `UserBotLatencyObserver` measures `VADUserStoppedSpeakingFrame → BotStartedSpeakingFrame` and emits a typed `LatencyBreakdown` with per-service `ttfb` entries, a `text_aggregation` slice, `user_turn_secs` (explicitly including VAD silence detection, STT finalization and any turn-analyzer wait), per-`function_calls` durations and a `chronological_events()` helper; accumulators are cleared on `InterruptionFrame` so stale metrics from cancelled cycles are discarded, and a separate one-shot `on_first_bot_speech_latency` measures greeting cold start from `ClientConnectedFrame`. `PipelineWorker` auto-wires this: `enable_turn_tracking=True` appends a `TurnTrackingObserver`, `enable_tracing=True` adds `UserBotLatencyObserver` and `TurnTraceObserver`, and `enable_rtvi=True` (the default) constructs an `RTVIProcessor` and its observer — so RTVI observability is on unless you turn it off. TWO HONEST LIMITS. First, Pipecat states NO perceptual target numbers anywhere — `README.md` says only 'Ultra-low latency interaction', and the one latency constant in the eval harness is a deliberately generous 60-second test timeout — so the familiar ~200 ms and ~800 ms figures are external voice-UX knowledge and must not be attributed to this source. But the learner's own CLAUDE.md does state one: P50 at or below 1.0 s and P95 at or below 1.5 s, measured from the last voiced user sample to the first audible assistant sample, including end-of-turn time. That is the line every bar in this chapter is drawn against. Second, collection is provided and AGGREGATION IS LEFT TO YOU — `examples/observability/` holds exactly three files and there is no dashboard, exporter or aggregation example in the repo. Both boson stacks are near-blind here: the gateway's only timing code is a trace decorator plus the ad-hoc `elapsed_ms` threaded into barge-in policy, and realtime_voice's single metric counter (`BoundedAudioOutput.discarded_frames`) is read by nothing. THE HANDOFF TO CH-12 is explicit and is the reason for the reordering: any processor placed serially between transcript and LLM lands on the critical path and must be wrapped in `start_processing_metrics()`/`stop_processing_metrics()` so its cost appears as a `ProcessingMetricsData` entry inside `LatencyBreakdown` rather than as an unexplained gap. The chapter ends by leaving a named, empty slot in the budget — 'rule evaluation, TBD ms' — and by stating the one number that must be benchmarked before any budget claim about Lina is credible: Korean STT on 8 kHz μ-law telephony audio has NO entry in `stt_latency.py` and must be measured and passed as `ttfs_p99_latency=`. (Deployment and process topology are NOT in this chapter — they are unrelated to latency accounting and belong to ch-04's worker topology and ch-13's deployment section.)

A provider control REFERENCES the 23-constant `stt_latency.py` table built in ch-06's `turn-boundary.html` rather than rebuilding it: it is a plain read-only dropdown of provider names with their constants, no bar chart, no Korean filter, no external-endpointing strip, and a caption linking back to ch-06 as the place that table lives — choosing Deepgram (0.35) versus xAI (2.14) moves the bar by 1.79 s, and a `stop_secs` slider shows the `max(0, TTFS_p99 - stop_secs)` safety net collapsing to zero. THE RULE KNOB IS DELIBERATELY EMPTY AND LABELLED 'TBD — you will price this in ch-12': dragging it shows the budget bending but the figure supplies no default value, so the learner arrives at ch-12 owning the denominator and not the answer. Beside the waterfall, an OBSERVER PLANE view draws the same pipeline a second time as a read-only layer above it: every `on_push_frame` and `on_process_frame` event firing as frames move, `can_generate_metrics()` returning `False` greying out the services that report nothing, and a live `LatencyBreakdown` object assembling itself field by field — `user_turn_secs`, per-service `ttfb`, `text_aggregation`, `function_calls` — with an `InterruptionFrame` button that clears the accumulators mid-turn so the reader sees why cancelled cycles do not pollute the numbers. A wrap-in-metrics toggle on any processor shows its cost appearing as a `ProcessingMetricsData` entry versus vanishing into an unexplained gap. Presets reproduce three budgets for comparison: boson's current text path, realtime_voice with unary ASR (the full transcription RTT landing on the critical path after VAD stop), and Pipecat with streaming STT. A TTFB-versus-TTFA toggle exposes the `leading_silence` term that byte-level monitoring hides, and a TTFB-versus-TTFAT toggle exposes reasoning tokens stopping the wrong clock. An 8 kHz Korean row is drawn as a visibly empty bar with a 'no number exists in this tree — measure it' annotation.

chapters.title: Rule Layers as Middleware: Designing boson's Rules onto Pipecat
chapters.summary: The chapter the learner asked for, placed AFTER the budget so its central trade-off can be priced rather than asserted. THE DECISIVE FINDING, verified in source and kept front and centre because it is what makes the whole design possible: FLOWS DOES NOT REQUIRE TRANSITIONS TO BE LLM FUNCTION CALLS. There are two independent producers of a `NodeConfig`. Path A is an LLM tool call whose handler returns `(result, next_node)`, resolved through `_create_transition_func` (manager.py:443) and gated by `_check_and_execute_transition` (:525), which fires only when `not assistant_aggregator.has_function_calls_in_progress` so a parallel tool batch cannot transition mid-batch. Path B is plain code calling the PUBLIC `await flow_manager.set_node_from_config(node_config)` (manager.py:588) from any coroutine — proven in-tree twice, at `examples/flows/warm_transfer.py:261` (called from a Daily transport callback guarded on `flow_manager.current_node`) and `examples/flows/multi_worker_handoff.py:352` (re-seeding a node from `@worker.event_handler("on_activated")`). So boson's deterministic chain — `RuleEngine.evaluate` → `Action` → `ExecutionResult.pending_transition` → `core._apply_stage_transition` → `StageMachine.transition` — ports directly, with a rule processor holding a `flow_manager` reference and calling `set_node_from_config(node_for(target))`. The model never gains control of the stage machine. THIS CHAPTER GIVES CONSTRAINTS, NOT CONCLUSIONS. The learner is handed three facts and asked to derive the design before any answer is shown. >>> AUTHORING CONSTRAINT — MANDATORY, NOT ADVISORY, AND THE SINGLE MOST IMPORTANT INSTRUCTION IN THIS CHAPTER SPEC. The prose in `read.md` MUST be written in the following order, and an authoring agent that emits the conclusions earlier has produced a chapter that fails its own purpose, because a derivation whose answer appears three sentences after the question is theatre. STEP 1 — state the three constraints below, each with its source file and line, and STOP. No seam, no collapse, no pipeline listing, no processor names, no `BosonRuleProcessor` code, not even as a forward promise phrased as an answer. STEP 2 — pose exactly two questions in the text and leave them open on the page: (i) WHERE IS THE SEAM — at which single position in a Pipecat pipeline does a complete user turn exist while inference has not yet begun? and (ii) MUST THE LAYERS COLLAPSE — can boson's cross-layer veto survive being spread across N adjacent processors, or not? Both questions must be posed BEFORE any sentence that answers either. STEP 3 — require the learner, in the text, to open and work `figures/rule-processor-placement.html` and place both blocks himself, and say plainly that the reveal button in that figure is disabled until he has. STEP 4 — ONLY NOW state the two conclusions (the seam is downstream of the user aggregator and upstream of the LLM; all layers must collapse into one processor), the mapping table, the recommended pipeline listing, and the ~40-line `BosonRuleProcessor.process_frame` body — all four of them framed explicitly and in so many words as the CHECK on his derivation, not as the lesson, with the standing rule that if his answer disagrees with a row then one of the two is wrong and the row names the source line that settles it. The ~40-line code body belongs in STEP 4 and MUST NOT appear in STEP 1; showing the implementation alongside the constraints hands over the seam and the collapse simultaneously and destroys both questions at once. <<< CONSTRAINT ONE: boson's rules provably need a FINISHED user utterance — `LayerPipeline.process(..., content: str, ...)` takes a plain `str`, every partial-transcript branch in the gateway ends in `continue`, and `end_signal.py` does whole-string `kw in lower` matching that would misfire on a prefix. CONSTRAINT TWO: `push_frame` is IRREVERSIBLE — there is no un-push, no retraction frame, and a frame that has left your processor is already being handled downstream. CONSTRAINT THREE, the data dependency that decides everything: `push_aggregation()` calls `self._context.add_message({...})` at :863 and only THEN `await self.push_context_frame()` at :866, while on the service side `src/pipecat/services/openai/base_llm.py` tests `isinstance(frame, LLMContextFrame)` at :601 and then, BEFORE any inference, already pushes `LLMFullResponseStartFrame()` at :603 and starts metrics at :604, with the completion itself beginning only at :605 (`await self._process_context(frame.context)`). Those two intervening lines matter to the derivation: by the time the completion starts, a frame has ALREADY left the LLM service downstream, so :601 -> :605 is not an empty window you can reach into — it is a window in which an irreversible push has already happened. FROM THOSE THREE, THE LEARNER DERIVES TWO THINGS. (a) THE SEAM: there is exactly one position where the complete turn exists and inference has not started — downstream of the user aggregator, upstream of the LLM — and rollback there is real, via a snapshot plus `context.set_messages(snapshot)`. Two rival positions must be knocked out by the learner, not by the text: an event handler on `on_user_turn_message_added` fires at :871, AFTER `push_context_frame()` at :866, so it is a notification that can never veto; and letting generation start and then cancelling pays the first TTFT twice and may have already spoken audio. (b) THE COLLAPSE: boson's `LayerPipeline` is a genuine two-phase commit where a `Filter` from ANY later layer rolls back every staged effect including the appended user message, deleted by OBJECT IDENTITY — but `push_frame` is irreversible and `LLMContext` offers only `set_messages(list)` with no identity handle, so cross-layer veto cannot survive being spread across N processors. ALL LAYERS MUST COLLAPSE INTO ONE PROCESSOR. That is the single structural cost of the port and the learner should reach it from constraints two and three before reading it. ONLY THEN comes THE MAPPING TABLE, presented explicitly as the CHECK on his derivation rather than as the lesson — if his answer disagrees with a row, one of them is wrong and the row names which source line settles it: `@check` sequential-with-short-circuit and `@check(mode="parallel")` `asyncio.gather` port verbatim as processor internals (Pipecat ships no rule scheduler, so there is nothing to fight); `Respond(text)` becomes pushing a `TTSSpeakFrame` and swallowing the context frame (Flows' `tts_say` only fires at node-set time, too coarse); `Inject(content)` becomes `context.add_message(...)` before pushing, losing the merge-into-the-last-user-message option that has no frame equivalent; `PreTool(name, args, preamble)` becomes a Flows `function` pre-action, which is exactly right because `function` actions ALWAYS wait (actions.py:285), matching boson's synchronous-before-generation semantics, with the preamble demoted to a separate `tts_say`; `Compact()` becomes a pre-action calling boson's compactor rather than Flows' 5-second summary path; `_GLOBAL_TOOLS` maps onto `FlowManager(global_functions=[...])`; `ScriptEngine.process_turn` runs unchanged inside the processor and is the cleanest port in the system; and `Continue()` / `Pass()` / `Filter(reason)` have NO HOME as actions at all — pre-LLM routing verdicts belong in the processor, because by the time an action runs the message is already in the context. THE CHAPTER MUST SHOW CODE, roughly forty real lines of a `BosonRuleProcessor.process_frame` body, because naming a class is not designing one: the mandatory `await super().process_frame(frame, direction)` as the literal first line; an unconditional drop of `InterimTranscriptionFrame` in the companion `BosonFillerGate` (or every keyword rule fires on prefixes); the `isinstance(frame, LLMContextFrame)` branch taking `snapshot = frame.context.get_messages()` before anything runs; the two-tier `await` — Tier 1 the 11 deterministic checks inline, Tier 2 the 2 `check_type="llm"` checks under `asyncio.gather`; the rollback path calling `frame.context.set_messages(snapshot)` on a `Filter` verdict; and the swallow-on-transition branch that calls `await self._flow_manager.set_node_from_config(node)` and RETURNS WITHOUT pushing the context frame. The `custom-processor-guide` excerpt is the model for that body and is finally cashed here. THE LATENCY BILL, now priceable because ch-11 built the budget: Tier 1 is pure Python and sub-millisecond; Tier 2 is `intent_rules` and `sentiment_tracker`, both `mode="parallel"` so wall clock is max not sum, and costs ~250-400 ms of added pre-LLM latency on EVERY turn. Drop that into ch-11's empty 'rule evaluation' slot against the 0.35-0.45 s Deepgram reference and the learner can see for himself that Tier 2 roughly doubles the pre-LLM half of the budget, and can state the trade in one sentence for the product owner: veto and in-turn steering cost 250-400 ms; next-turn transitions cost 0 ms; boson pays the 250-400 ms today. Wrap the processor in `start_processing_metrics()`/`stop_processing_metrics()` or the bill never appears in `LatencyBreakdown`. THE PIPELINE the learner should arrive at, with every position justified by data dependency rather than taste: `transport.input(), stt, BosonFillerGate(), user_aggregator, BosonRuleProcessor(...), llm, tts, transport.output(), assistant_aggregator` — with `FlowManager` NOT in the list. `BosonFillerGate` must sit between `stt` and `user_aggregator` because it needs `TranscriptionFrame` text that only `stt` produces and must drop it before the aggregator commits it; one position earlier it sees only audio and the rule is dead, one later the '네' is already `add_message`d and a one-line string check has become a rollback. `assistant_aggregator` stays after `transport.output()`, and boson has the same invariant for a different reason: a `Respond()` interrupted mid-TTS must not be recorded as spoken. On a transition turn the rule processor SWALLOWS the context frame and lets the Flows node be the sole inference trigger — and this deliberately reverses the naive advice, because ordering `set_node_from_config()` before `push_frame()` does not fix the race: the node's frames enter at the pipeline HEAD and must traverse stt → gate → aggregator, while your pushed frame reaches the llm immediately. Swallowing removes the race by construction. FOUR REAL FRICTIONS, none fatal: transition LEGALITY is lost (`StageDefinition.transitions` and `TransitionResult(success=False, ...)` have no counterpart and there is no node registry, so keep boson's `StageMachine` as a pure pre-check validator in front of `set_node_from_config`); every Flows transition is an INFERENCE TRIGGER by default, so ported nodes need `respond_immediately=False`; there is no silent transition at all, since `LLMSetToolsFrame` always fires and `task_messages` is required, making `task_messages=[]` the closest no-op; and ordering becomes QUEUE ordering rather than call ordering. THE BUS AS A SIDE CHANNEL, and when it is the wrong tool: the bus is name-addressed pub/sub between WORKERS with a one-way callback and NO READ API — no `bus.get()`, no snapshot, no query — plus two queue hops of staleness, while boson's layers need synchronous reads of live state (`SharedLayerContext.__getattr__`/`__setattr__` proxy straight through to the live `SessionState`, `AgentStatusTracker.get_status()` is a poll, `SignalQueue.get_recent()` is a query), so porting them onto the bus would silently turn `session.counter += 1` into a write to a local replica. Pipecat's own answer for non-adjacent coordination is the `VoicemailDetector` pattern — three shared `EventNotifier()` objects handed to four processors — and for cross-cutting observation it is the ch-11 observer plane, which sees every frame at every processor without being spliced in. Reserve the bus for genuine process boundaries and for `WorkerRegistry.watch(name, handler)`. Three open risks close the chapter with named prototypes: the filler-filter-versus-energy-barge-in gap (measure the delta between interruption broadcast and `TranscriptionFrame` arrival over lone Korean backchannels on 8 kHz audio; a positive gap mandates a custom `BaseUserTurnStartStrategy` that withholds turn-start until a transcript exists), the transition frame race (assert with a `FrameLogger` at the llm input that exactly ONE inference-triggering frame arrives per turn and that `LLMSetToolsFrame` precedes it — watching for both zero and two), and the two-phase-commit blast radius (snapshot/restore around the whole rule round, replay the Lina e2e suite, count divergences, specifically turns where a `PreTool` appended synthetic tool-call history before a later layer filtered).
chapters.figure_spec: A DERIVATION bench, not an answer key: the tool withholds the recommended pipeline until the learner has placed the processors himself. MIRRORING THE CHAPTER'S AUTHORING CONSTRAINT, and binding on this figure too: nothing in the initial render may state the seam, the collapse, the recommended processor order or the `BosonRuleProcessor` body. Those live behind gates that open only after the learner has acted — the mapping table behind both blocks being placed, PANEL FOUR's code view behind PANEL TWO's veto verdict having been computed at least once — and every gated surface is labelled CHECK YOUR DERIVATION when it opens. If the figure is loaded and read top to bottom without interaction, it must give the answer away nowhere. PANEL ONE opens with an EMPTY pipeline containing only `transport.input(), stt, user_aggregator, llm, tts, transport.output(), assistant_aggregator` and two unplaced blocks, `BosonFillerGate` and `BosonRuleProcessor`. A 'reveal the mapping table' button stays disabled until both blocks have been placed, and when opened it is labelled CHECK YOUR DERIVATION, with each of the 11 rows citing the source line that settles it. PANEL THREE is the two-phase commit: run four layers staging actions, fire a `Filter` from the last one, and animate boson's identity-based rollback deleting the appended user message — then re-run the same round as four separate Pipecat processors and mark, in red, every frame that already escaped `push_frame` and cannot be recalled, which is the proof that all layers must collapse into one object. PANEL FOUR is a live CODE view of the ~40-line `BosonRuleProcessor.process_frame` body, syntax-highlighted and steppable, with the mandatory `super().process_frame(frame, direction)` first line, the `InterimTranscriptionFrame` drop, the `snapshot = frame.context.get_messages()` capture, the two-tier `await`, the `set_messages(snapshot)` rollback and the swallow-on-transition `return` — each line highlighting as the frame reaches it, and a 'delete the super() call' switch that reproduces the ch-01 black hole. PANEL FIVE is the latency bill dropped into ch-11's empty slot: 11 deterministic checks as a sub-millisecond sliver against 2 parallel LLM checks at 250-400 ms, laid over the Deepgram 0.35-0.45 s reference, with an in-turn-veto versus next-turn-transition switch that moves the stage change one turn later and the bar to zero, and a metrics toggle showing the cost appearing in `LatencyBreakdown` or vanishing. PANEL SIX is the transition race: fire a rule-driven transition and count inference-triggering frames arriving at the llm input — push the context frame AND call `set_node_from_config` to get two generations, swallow both to get zero, swallow only the context frame to get exactly one — with `LLMSetToolsFrame` ordering asserted on the same trace.

chapters.title: Capstone: Keep or Replace, Subsystem by Subsystem
chapters.summary: THE ONLY PLACE IN THIS COURSE WHERE A VOTE IS CAST. Twelve chapters produced mechanism and evidence and deliberately withheld verdicts; this one converts all of it into a per-subsystem KEEP realtime_voice / ADOPT Pipecat / HYBRID-WRAP decision. The chapter is graded on being DECIDABLE, and that is a hard requirement, not a style note. An earlier draft of this capstone conditioned its answer on four numbers the course itself proves nobody has — Korean STT accuracy on 8 kHz μ-law, the interruption-broadcast-to-transcript gap, the Tier-2 rule latency against a real endpoint, and a one-inference-per-turn assertion — with the result that its honest output was 'a plan to decide' and nothing could be graded. THREE RULES FIX THAT. RULE ONE: every row gets a COMMITMENT, made under EXPLICITLY STATED assumptions. Not 'depends'; a vote, plus the sentence 'I am assuming X'. RULE TWO: every row gets a written FALSIFIER — the specific observation that would overturn that vote. the SHAPE, using a deliberately unowned example so the illustration does not steer a row: a vote of the form 'adopt X for row N' is falsified by 'on our own corpus, X produces more false turn-starts than what we run today', and a vote of the form 'keep Y for row N' is falsified by 'the measurement shows Y costs more than the budget allows'. Note that both example falsifiers name an OBSERVATION, not a preference. If a row cannot be falsified by any observation, the vote is not a decision and the row is mis-stated. RULE THREE: exactly ONE measurement is actually RUN, not listed — the Tier-2 rule-latency probe from ch-12, chosen precisely because it is the only one of the four that needs no telephony carrier, no Korean STT contract and no audio at all. IT HAS A REAL EXECUTABLE HOME, and this is a hard requirement because a self-contained offline HTML file loaded from `file://` cannot call a model endpoint and must never be assigned a job it structurally cannot do: the probe ships as `wiki/courses/pipecat/ch-13/tier2-probe.py`, a standalone runnable script that instantiates the two `check_type="llm"` checks (`intent_rules`, `sentiment_tracker`), runs them under `asyncio.gather` over a corpus of real Lina user turns against the learner's own model endpoint, and prints P50/P95 wall clock in milliseconds on stdout. The learner runs `python3 ch-13/tier2-probe.py`, copies the two numbers, and PASTES them into the input fields in `figures/migration-map.html`; the figure then renders measured-versus-ghost-estimate from the pasted value and does no network I/O of any kind. That number either lands inside the 250-400 ms estimate ch-12 used or it does not, and either way the budget row becomes decided rather than pending. The other three measurements stay as falsifiers with owners and preconditions, which is the honest place for them. THE ROWS — SEVENTEEN of them, each with vote + assumption + falsifier, and this count is fixed: (1) VAD; (2) ASR/streaming STT; (3) TTS and the six-service Korean word-timestamp intersection; (4) `KoreanPhraseChunker`; (5) `AudioTextPlayoutLedger`; (6) transport; (7) telephony serializer; (8) session auth (`WebRTCSessionManager`); (9) control protocol (`ControlEvent`); (10) the LLM loop; (11) tools; (12) the stage machine; (13) the rule layers; (14) `ScriptEngine`; (15) compaction; (16) observability; and (17) DEPLOYMENT AND PROCESS TOPOLOGY, which is a full row like any other and not a postscript. Every mention of the row count in this chapter and in its figure reads SEVENTEEN. THE EVIDENCE DIGEST, which is what twelve chapters actually produced, and which is where this chapter's prose stops. FOR EACH ROW the chapter states which chapter supplied which mechanism fact, and the VOTE CELL IS LEFT EMPTY — the chapter states the rows and the evidence and NEVER the verdict, because RULE ONE demands the learner commit and an outline that commits for him has cancelled the only graded exercise in the course. Write the digest with no comparative adjective anywhere in it: no 'better', no 'wins', no 'should use', no 'the right choice', and no REPLACE/KEEP/ADOPT label attached to any row by the text. Row 1, VAD — ch-06 supplied both mechanisms in full: four states with a `min_volume` AND-gate, a `STARTING → QUIET` path, native 8 kHz with identical six-chunk counts at 16 kHz/512 and 8 kHz/256, and `audio_idle_timeout`, against a two-state bool at `threshold=0.5` with no volume gate, no idle timeout, and a hard 16 kHz-only `ValueError`; plus the observed two-frame-blip divergence. Row 2, ASR — ch-03 supplied `OpenAICompatibleUnaryASR` buffering to WAV for one blocking `finalize()` call, ch-06 supplied streaming STT plus the 23-constant `stt_latency.py` spread and the smart-turn default, and ch-11 supplied the arithmetic that places a unary transcription RTT wholly after VAD stop on the critical path, against the learner's own P50 1.0 s / P95 1.5 s line. Row 3, TTS — ch-07 supplied the twelve `Language.KO` services, the six-service intersection with word-timestamp emission, the provenance caveat that six is a grep over declared capability and not a behavioural verification, `resolve_language`'s silent fallback, and the absence of any maintained self-hosted Korean TTS. Row 4, `KoreanPhraseChunker` — ch-03 supplied the 283-line algorithm and ch-07 supplied the fact that `SimpleTextAggregator` plus `UNAMBIGUOUS_SENTENCE_ENDING_PUNCTUATION` is what Pipecat offers in its place and that Korean falls through the CJK branch untested. Row 5, `AudioTextPlayoutLedger` — ch-03 supplied `audible_text()` and `playout_complete()`, ch-08 supplied Pipecat's position-based alternative and the untagged-partial gap, and ch-07 supplied the six-service dependency that determines whether the alternative is even available. Row 6, transport — ch-05 supplied that ~960 lines of realtime_voice's aiortc transport land where `SmallWebRTCTransport` lands on the same library, plus renegotiation and ICE restart on one side only. Row 7, telephony serializer — ch-05 supplied that there is no telephony transport at all, that a phone call is `FastAPIWebsocketTransport` plus one of 6 telephony serializers, that neither existing stack has any telephony path, and that a Korean carrier outside those 6 means a ~250-300 line `FrameSerializer`; ch-06 supplied that the 8 kHz side costs no VAD retuning and that no 8 kHz Korean STT number exists in the tree. Row 8, session auth — ch-03 and ch-05 supplied `WebRTCSessionManager`'s HMAC digest, 15-minute TTL and one-live-peer `SessionConflictError`, and that Pipecat ships no counterpart. Row 9, control protocol — ch-03 and ch-05 supplied `ControlEvent` v1's dotted-type validation, strict in-order sequence checking, 64 KiB cap and recursive audio rejection, and that Pipecat ships no counterpart. Row 10, the LLM loop — ch-09 supplied all of it: the live-list `get_messages()` against boson's `deepcopy`, one inference per `LLMContextFrame`, no `max_turns` anywhere, the loop closed by topology, and the three costed resolutions (adopt / wrap / bypass) that ch-09 explicitly left unresolved. Row 11, tools — ch-09 supplied the three registration routes, the `result_callback` contract, `run_in_parallel=True`, the 22 tool signatures, the absent tool role in boson's `Message.role`, and boson's three separate gates that Pipecat's registry has no slot for. Row 12, the stage machine — ch-10 supplied `FlowManager` as a plain class outside the pipeline, the absence of `FlowConfig`, the two `NodeConfig` producers, the absence of transition-legality validation and of a node registry, and `stage_config.py`'s direct mapping with `transitions` and `skills` unmapped. Row 13, the rule layers — ch-12 supplied the three constraints, the seam derivation, the collapse argument, the 11-row mapping table and the Tier-2 latency bill this chapter is about to measure. Row 14, `ScriptEngine` — ch-12 supplied that `process_turn` runs unchanged inside a processor. Row 15, compaction — the excerpt supplies `LLMContextSummarizer` and `LLMAutoContextSummarizationConfig` against `gateway/compact/`, the three-way parameter correspondence, and the two named losses (no pre/post compact hooks, and the `<system-reminder>Active stage: ...</system-reminder>` re-injection that must be re-attached explicitly). Row 16, observability — ch-11 supplied the observer plane, `LatencyBreakdown`, `can_generate_metrics()` gating and the fact that aggregation is left to you, against two stacks whose only metrics are a trace decorator, an ad-hoc `elapsed_ms` and a counter nothing reads. Row 17, deployment topology — ch-04 supplied the `WorkerRunner(auto_end=False)` host shape, and this chapter's own deployment section supplies the rest. THE TWO IRREDUCIBLE COLLISIONS ARE STATED AS ROWS WITH THEIR EVIDENCE AND ARE NOT RESOLVED BY THE TEXT. First, the agent boundary (rows 10 and 11): adopting Pipecat's pipeline means Pipecat owns the LLM call and the tool loop, which stands against the learner's own contract that Basement and Gateway stay text-native — ch-09 costed three shapes and named none, and the priced consequences that attach to whichever the learner picks are the missing turn ceiling (rebuildable as a counting processor over `FunctionCallsStartedFrame`) and the `{"role": "tool"}` schema rewrite at 22 signatures. Second, the rule layers (row 13): ch-12's derivation produced a seam and a collapse, and the open question this chapter must pose without answering is how much of boson survives unedited under each vote — the candidate shape the learner is asked to evaluate, not told to adopt, is one `BosonRuleProcessor` between `user_aggregator` and `llm` holding all 13 checks, the `RuleEngine`, the `SignalQueue` and a real `SessionState`, with `StageMachine` kept as a pure legality pre-check and `FlowManager` driving stages from outside via `set_node_from_config`. Both collisions get a vote cell, an assumption cell and a falsifier cell, all three filled by the learner. WHAT HAS NO PIPECAT HOME and must stay boson code: cross-layer veto, transition legality, `StageDefinition.skills`, per-session attribute namespaces, the `TOOL_PROCESSING` status, and the `<system-reminder>` protocol. WHAT PIPECAT GIVES BACK, including the two pieces routed here from earlier chapters: Flows nodes for stages, `global_functions` for `_GLOBAL_TOOLS`, `function` pre-actions for `PreTool`, `ContextStrategy.RESET` as per-transition context truncation boson does not have today, the ch-11 observer plane for a stack that is currently near-blind, and COMPACTION — split out of ch-09 because it is a different subsystem with different failure modes: `LLMContextSummarizer` plus `LLMAutoContextSummarizationConfig` covers what `gateway/compact/` does, parameter for parameter (`threshold_messages=30 → max_unsummarized_messages`, `keep_recent=10 → min_messages_after_summary`, plus a token trigger boson never had), with two real losses that belong on the give-back row's falsifier line — pre/post compact hooks have no equivalent, and the `<system-reminder>Active stage: ...</system-reminder>` re-injection in `swap_compact` must be re-attached explicitly or stage identity is silently lost at every compaction. THE DEPLOYMENT AND PROCESS TOPOLOGY, absorbed here from the old latency chapter because it is a decision input and not a latency term, and building on the Lina host topology ch-04 already delivered: Pipecat ships a DEVELOPMENT runner (its own banner says so, and there are no deployment docs in the repo), `main()` ends at a single `uvicorn.run(app, ...)` with no `workers=`, every session is an `asyncio.Task` on one loop with no admission control or per-session CPU isolation, the real runtime unit is the worker under `WorkerRunner(auto_end=False)`, cross-process scale-out is the bus rather than the runner, cold start is `setup()` and not `StartFrame` (measured by `StartupTimingObserver`, with processors set up concurrently so the total is a span not a sum), and the entire scaling configuration surface is one `min_agents = 1` line in the generated `pcc-deploy.toml`. The concrete choice — one long-lived process versus container-per-call with a warm pool sized to concurrent-call peak — is ROW 17 of the seventeen, with its own vote, assumption and falsifier cells like every other row, and `GatewayCore`'s process-scoped MCP subprocesses must be re-hosted above the worker so they are not respawned per session. THE DELIVERABLES: the completed seventeen-row vote table with assumptions and falsifiers; the target architecture drawn end to end with `FlowManager` outside the processor list; a migration sequence that keeps the agent shippable at every step, ordered by the learner and defended in one sentence per step; `ch-13/tier2-probe.py` itself, run at least once, with its printed P50/P95 pasted into the figure and what that did to the ch-11 budget; and the remaining falsifiers written as a watchlist with owners, not as a reason to postpone the decision.
chapters.figure_spec: A DECISION LEDGER that refuses to stay undecided. SEVENTEEN subsystem rows — VAD, ASR, TTS, chunking, playout ledger, transport, telephony serializer, session auth, control protocol, LLM loop, tools, stage machine, rule layers, script engine, compaction, observability, deployment topology — matching the seventeen rows the summary enumerates, with no row appearing in one list and not the other. Each row ships PRE-FILLED with its evidence digest (which chapter supplied which mechanism fact) and an EMPTY vote cell; the figure never suggests, defaults, pre-selects or highlights a vote, and contains no REPLACE/KEEP/ADOPT label that the learner did not click. Each row has THREE mandatory cells, not one: a vote (keep realtime_voice / adopt Pipecat / hybrid-wrap), a free-text ASSUMPTION, and a free-text FALSIFIER. A row with an empty assumption or falsifier is rendered incomplete in red, and the export button stays disabled until every row is complete, so 'it depends' is structurally unavailable. Each falsifier field offers the observation type it would need (corpus, probe, benchmark, code assertion) and marks whether that observation is available today. As votes are cast, the target architecture diagram, the line counts on each side, and the ch-11 latency budget update live. Incompatible combinations are flagged with the reason (adopt Pipecat's LLM service while keeping text-native Gateway tools; keep realtime_voice's Silero while adding telephony, which hard-rejects 8 kHz; drop `AudioTextPlayoutLedger` while choosing a TTS outside the six word-timestamp services — with the reminder that those six are a grep, not a behavioural test). A separate MEASUREMENT panel is real rather than aspirational, and it does NO network I/O — the figure is a self-contained offline `file://` page and cannot call a model endpoint, so the measurement lives in a sibling runnable script, `ch-13/tier2-probe.py`, which runs the two `check_type="llm"` checks (`intent_rules`, `sentiment_tracker`) under `asyncio.gather` over a corpus of real Lina turns against the learner's own endpoint and prints P50/P95 in milliseconds. The panel shows the exact command to run, two numeric input fields for the printed P50 and P95, and stays in an explicit UNMEASURED state — greyed, with the run instruction as its only content — until both are pasted. Once pasted it draws the measured bar with the ch-12 250-400 ms estimate as a ghost bar behind it, and writes the measured value into ch-11's previously empty 'rule evaluation' slot so the whole waterfall re-renders with a real number in it. The pasted values persist in `localStorage` so a reload does not discard the one measurement the capstone is graded on. The three unrun measurements appear beneath it as a watchlist with owners and preconditions, explicitly styled as falsifiers rather than blockers. Each row carries an evidence link back to the chapter and excerpt that supplied its mechanism, and the tool emits four artifacts: the completed vote table, the target-architecture processor list with `FlowManager` drawn outside it, the deployment topology as voted in row 17 (one long-lived `WorkerRunner(auto_end=False)` process versus container-per-call with a warm pool), and the learner's own migration sequence with his one-sentence defence of each step's position.
